sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A database stores organized data. In a relational database, data is arranged in tables: each row describes one item, such as a customer, and each column holds one kind of information, such as their name.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Applications need to store and find information reliably. A database management system, or DBMS, manages that work. PostgreSQL is the DBMS you will use in this course; SQL is the language used to give it instructions.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A table defines column names and data types, such as text or dates. A query asks for a result from those tables. Reading data with SELECT does not change the stored rows.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: SELECT * asks for every column. FROM customers chooses the table. ORDER BY id sorts the result by customer ID, from smallest to largest. The semicolon ends the statement.
sections.code: SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The query lists all customers. Read across a row to see one customer's details; read down a column to compare the same detail across customers.
sections.code: SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The orders example selects only the information needed for an order list: its ID, customer, date, status, and total. Naming the columns makes that list explicit.
sections.code: SELECT id, customer_id, ordered_on, status, total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The Retail dataset contains six customers. NULL means a value is missing; t and f display the Boolean values true and false. The rows appear in ID order.

id | name | city | email | joined_on | vip
— | — | — | — | — | —
1 | Ada | London | ada@example.test | 2024-01-05 | t
2 | Ben | Paris | ben@example.test | 2024-02-10 | f
3 | Cleo | London | NULL | 2024-02-20 | f
4 | Davi | Berlin | davi@example.test | 2024-03-01 | t
5 | Eli | NULL | eli@example.test | 2024-03-15 | f
6 | Fara | Paris | fara@example.test | 2024-04-01 | f

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A table has no guaranteed row order. Use ORDER BY when order matters. A missing value, shown as NULL, is different from the number zero or an empty string.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Start by distinguishing stored data from a query result: a query can select, calculate, and arrange what you see without rearranging the underlying table.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: For each query, first identify the table and required columns. Compare the result headings with your SELECT list, then check that ORDER BY gives the requested row order.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A table stores rows with named columns. PostgreSQL manages the database; SQL describes what to retrieve. SELECT chooses output, FROM chooses its source, and ORDER BY controls row order.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A key identifies a row so other data can refer to it reliably. A primary key is unique and never NULL. A foreign key requires a matching referenced key when its value is present.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Names can repeat or change. Storing a customer ID in an order keeps the relationship clear without copying the customer's details into every order.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Here, customers.id identifies a customer and orders.customer_id refers to it. One customer can have many orders. A guest order may have NULL customer_id. In order_items, the pair (order_id, product_id) identifies a row.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: SELECT id, name shows the identifier beside the readable name. FROM customers reads customer rows; ORDER BY id makes the list easy to check. This query reads existing keys; it does not create them.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The result puts each customer's ID beside their name. Other tables use the ID to refer to that customer, even if two people have the same name.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The order_items query shows both parts of its primary key. A product can appear in different orders, but the same order/product pair cannot appear twice in this table.
sections.code: SELECT order_id, product_id, quantity FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, product_id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Each customer has a different ID in this dataset. The name is descriptive; the primary key is what guarantees a unique reference.

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada
2 | Ben
3 | Cleo
4 | Davi
5 | Eli
6 | Fara

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A foreign key does not make its column unique: several orders may refer to the same customer. Nullable foreign keys permit missing references; NOT NULL is a separate rule.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A schema is a named container for database objects, such as tables. Keys describe row identity and relationships inside those tables; later JOIN lessons use those relationships to combine data.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace one customer ID into orders, then an order ID into order_items. Check which values may repeat and which whole key must remain unique.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys protect relationships. A relationship may be one-to-many, and a key can contain more than one column.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An expression produces a value, such as a number, a comparison result, or a calculation using columns. SQL describes the result you want; PostgreSQL chooses how to obtain it.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Calculating values in a query keeps the calculation close to the data. You can ask for each order line's revenue without storing another copy of a value that can be calculated.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For a typical SELECT, think: choose sources with FROM, filter with WHERE, group and filter groups, calculate output, remove duplicates, sort, then limit. This explains meaning; the database's execution plan may perform work differently.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: SELECT 2 + 3 * 4 evaluates an expression without needing a table. Multiplication happens before addition. AS answer names the output column; parentheses can change arithmetic grouping.
sections.code: SELECT 2 + 3 * 4 AS answer;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The query returns one row with answer = 14. To get 20 instead, the arithmetic would need (2 + 3) * 4; parentheses express the intended calculation.
sections.code: SELECT 2 + 3 * 4 AS answer;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The order_items query calculates quantity * unit_price separately for each line and labels it revenue. The original quantity and price columns remain unchanged.
sections.code: SELECT order_id, product_id, quantity * unit_price AS revenue FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, product_id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The one output value is 14. There is no FROM clause because this calculation uses only literal numbers, not stored rows.

answer
—
14

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: An alias created in SELECT is unavailable in the same query's WHERE; repeat the expression or use a later query layer. Integer division drops the fractional part, so cast an operand before dividing when needed.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Expressions underpin filters, computed columns, and aggregates. Logical query order also explains why ORDER BY can use a SELECT alias while WHERE cannot.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Work out each expression by hand before running it. Check operator precedence, the result name, and whether integer or decimal arithmetic matches the question.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Expressions calculate values; aliases name their output. Understand the logical stages of a query, while letting PostgreSQL choose its physical execution plan.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: SELECT can return only the columns you need, in the order you choose. This is called projection. A column alias is a temporary name for a column in the query result.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A focused result is easier to read and gives an application predictable column names. It also avoids transferring columns that the application does not use.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: List columns or expressions after SELECT, separated by commas. AS gives an output a readable name. An alias changes the result heading; it does not rename the stored column.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: name AS product displays name under the heading product, and price AS unit_price does the same for price. FROM products chooses the table. ORDER BY id sorts by an input column that is not displayed.
sections.code: SELECT name AS product, price AS unit_price FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example returns two columns, product and unit_price, while keeping one row per product. The output column order follows the SELECT list.
sections.code: SELECT name AS product, price AS unit_price FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: An order report can call id order_number and shipped_on dispatch_date. Those labels describe the report without changing the orders table or its values.
sections.code: SELECT id AS order_number, shipped_on AS dispatch_date FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result has eight product rows. The headings come from the aliases; prices such as 12.50 are copied from the stored price column.

product | unit_price
— | —
Notebook | 12.50
Pen | 2.00
Keyboard | 75.00
Monitor | 250.00
Mug | 15.00
Lamp | 45.00
Cable | 8.00
Folder | 4.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Single quotes mean a text value; double quotes identify a name. Unquoted names become lowercase. SELECT * can unexpectedly add output columns after a table changes.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Projection chooses columns; WHERE chooses rows. An output alias can be used in ORDER BY, but it is not available to WHERE in the same query.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check both the number and order of output columns. Give calculated values clear aliases and verify that a renamed heading has not been confused with a text literal.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use an explicit SELECT list to shape a stable result. AS improves output names while leaving the source table unchanged.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: DISTINCT keeps one copy of each complete output row. Without it, SELECT normally retains duplicate rows, even when the displayed values look identical.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A list of available categories needs each category once, rather than one repeated category name for every product.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PostgreSQL evaluates the selected values, then removes rows whose values match in every output column. For this comparison, two NULLs count as equal. DISTINCT does not establish an output order.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: SELECT DISTINCT category returns unique category values. FROM products supplies the product rows. ORDER BY category sorts the remaining categories by the database's text ordering rules.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Several products share Office or Tech, but each category appears once in the result. Adding more products in an existing category will not add another category row.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The order example selects month number and status together. DISTINCT keeps each unique pair, so one month can appear several times if it contains different statuses.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT EXTRACT(MONTH FROM ordered_on)::integer AS month, status FROM orders ORDER BY month, status;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Home, Office, and Tech are the three category values in Retail. Their displayed order comes from ORDER BY, not from DISTINCT.

category
—
Home
Office
Tech

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Adding a unique product ID makes each selected row different, so DISTINCT no longer produces one row per category. Removing repeated rows can also hide an incorrect join rather than fix it.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: DISTINCT removes identical output rows; GROUP BY gathers rows so aggregates can summarize them. A month number alone combines different years, so include a year or month-start date in multi-year reports.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Decide what makes an entire result row unique. Compare a query selecting only category with one selecting category and id, and explain why the row counts differ.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: DISTINCT compares the whole selected row, including NULLs for duplicate removal. Choose the output columns carefully and use ORDER BY separately.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: ORDER BY sorts result rows. LIMIT sets the maximum number returned; OFFSET skips a number of rows before returning the next ones.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Top-price lists and result pages need a clear order. Without one, PostgreSQL is free to return any matching rows, and a page may change unexpectedly between runs.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ASC means ascending and is the default; DESC means descending. Multiple sort keys apply left to right. Add a unique key to resolve ties. PostgreSQL defaults to NULLS LAST for ASC and NULLS FIRST for DESC.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: ORDER BY price DESC, id sorts high prices first, then smaller IDs when prices tie. LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows of that order. DESC applies only to price here.
sections.code: SELECT id, name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC, id LIMIT 3;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example returns the three most expensive products. The ID tie-breaker ensures that equal prices do not make the choice unpredictable.
sections.code: SELECT id, name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC, id LIMIT 3;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The shipment report explicitly puts missing shipment dates first, then sorts known dates ascending. The final id key gives a stable order when several orders share a date.
sections.code: SELECT id, shipped_on FROM orders ORDER BY shipped_on NULLS FIRST, id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The top prices in Retail are Monitor at 250.00, Keyboard at 75.00, and Lamp at 45.00. This is a sorted selection, not insertion order.

id | name | price
— | — | —
4 | Monitor | 250.00
3 | Keyboard | 75.00
6 | Lamp | 45.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: LIMIT alone does not mean earliest inserted rows. Large OFFSET values still require skipping earlier rows, and changing data can shift page boundaries even with a stable sort.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Sorting is separate from filtering. For large changing lists, pagination based on the last seen sort key can avoid some problems of OFFSET; that approach also needs a complete, stable ordering.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check price ties, repeated dates, and missing dates. For page exercises, calculate which rows OFFSET skips before LIMIT selects the requested page.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Sort with ORDER BY, resolve ties explicitly, and choose NULL placement deliberately. LIMIT and OFFSET operate on that ordered result.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: WHERE decides which rows appear in a query result. Its condition must evaluate to true for a row to remain; false and unknown results are discarded.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Filtering at the database lets a report request only relevant products, orders, or customers, instead of retrieving everything and filtering elsewhere.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use = for equality, <> or != for inequality, and <, <=, >, >= for ordered comparisons. Compare compatible types. A comparison with NULL normally produces unknown, which does not pass WHERE.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: FROM products supplies rows. WHERE price < 20 keeps products below 20, excluding exactly 20. SELECT chooses their displayed columns, and ORDER BY id sorts the remaining rows.
sections.code: SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price < 20 ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small example shows inexpensive products only. It changes which rows are returned, not their stored prices or any other data.
sections.code: SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price < 20 ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The stock report uses <= 8, so products with exactly eight units are included. Sorting by stock then id places the lowest stock first with a clear tie-breaker.
sections.code: SELECT id, name, stock FROM products WHERE stock <= 8 ORDER BY stock, id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Five Retail products cost less than 20. The selected prices can be checked individually against the strict boundary; a price of 20 would not qualify.

id | name | price
— | — | —
1 | Notebook | 12.50
2 | Pen | 2.00
5 | Mug | 15.00
7 | Cable | 8.00
8 | Folder | 4.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: SQL equality uses =, not ==. Do not write price = NULL to find missing prices; use IS NULL. A chain such as 1 < price < 20 must be written as two comparisons.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: SELECT chooses columns while WHERE chooses rows. WHERE is applied before grouping; conditions on aggregate totals belong in HAVING, introduced later.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check values below, equal to, and above each boundary. Explain why < differs from <=, and confirm whether missing values should be included.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: WHERE keeps true conditions only. Choose comparison operators precisely and handle NULL explicitly when it matters to the question.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: AND combines conditions that must both hold. OR accepts at least one true condition. NOT reverses true and false; it leaves an unknown result unknown.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Business filters often require combinations, such as an available product in a chosen category, or an order that is neither pending nor cancelled.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: NOT has higher priority than AND, and AND has higher priority than OR. Parentheses show the intended groups. Do not rely on conditions running left to right: PostgreSQL may reorganize their evaluation.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: category = 'Office' AND stock > 0 requires both a matching category and positive stock. Single quotes delimit the text value Office. ORDER BY id arranges the matching products.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE category = 'Office' AND stock > 0 ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example includes only Office products that are in stock. A Tech product with plenty of stock still fails the category condition.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE category = 'Office' AND stock > 0 ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: NOT (status = 'pending' OR status = 'cancelled') excludes either unwanted status. The parentheses make NOT apply to the whole alternative, rather than only the first comparison.
sections.code: SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE NOT (status = 'pending' OR status = 'cancelled') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The three Retail matches are Notebook, Pen, and Folder. Every displayed row satisfies both parts of the AND condition.

id | name
— | —
1 | Notebook
2 | Pen
8 | Folder

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A OR B AND C means A OR (B AND C), not (A OR B) AND C. NULL also matters: false AND unknown is false, while true OR unknown is true.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Combined conditions build on ordinary comparisons and NULL rules. CASE can choose an output value by conditions; WHERE uses conditions to decide whether a row remains.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Rewrite each verbal rule with parentheses first. Test a row satisfying only one condition, and check whether a NULL input changes the result.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose AND for joint requirements, OR for alternatives, and NOT for negation. Parentheses and NULL-aware reasoning make combined filters reliable.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: IN checks whether a value matches one of several alternatives. BETWEEN checks an inclusive interval: both endpoints belong to it. A half-open interval includes its start but excludes its end.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: These forms keep category lists and date ranges readable. Half-open time periods fit together without overlap, such as June ending exactly where July starts.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: category IN ('Home','Office') means either category is acceptable. x BETWEEN a AND b means x >= a AND x <= b. For a month, >= its first day AND < the next month's first day avoids end-of-day assumptions.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The example filters category using IN, then returns product IDs and names. The comma separates alternatives inside the parentheses; it does not combine two requirements with AND.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE category IN ('Home','Office') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Products from either Home or Office qualify. A product does not need to belong to both categories, and Tech products are excluded.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE category IN ('Home','Office') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The order example covers June 2024 from June 1 inclusive to July 1 exclusive. DATE marks a typed date value and avoids interpreting a date as ordinary text.
sections.code: SELECT id, ordered_on FROM orders WHERE ordered_on >= DATE '2024-06-01' AND ordered_on < DATE '2024-07-01' ORDER BY id;

sections.body: BETWEEN includes its upper endpoint. For timestamps, an upper bound of June 30 at midnight misses most of that day. NOT IN can produce unknown if an unmatched list contains NULL.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A month number alone includes that month in every year. Explicit date boundaries express one particular period and also work when a date field later becomes a timestamp.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test the day before the start, the start itself, the last included day, and the next period's first instant. For lists, check matching, nonmatching, and missing values.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use IN for discrete alternatives and choose interval boundaries deliberately. BETWEEN is inclusive; >= start AND < end is convenient for adjacent time periods.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: NULL means that a value is missing or unknown. It is not zero, an empty string, or the text 'NULL'. For example, an absent shipment date does not tell us a date to compare.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Optional information needs a way to remain unknown. Treating an unknown city as a real city name would give misleading filters and reports.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Ordinary comparisons involving NULL produce unknown. WHERE keeps only true. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test presence. IS DISTINCT FROM provides inequality that always returns true or false, including for NULLs.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: email IS NULL finds customers without a known email. It is a presence test, not an equality comparison. The rest of the query selects their IDs and names in ID order.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE email IS NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Cleo has no email in Retail, so that customer is returned. A real empty string would count as a present value and would need a separate test.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE email IS NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: city IS DISTINCT FROM 'London' includes cities different from London and also NULL cities. In contrast, city <> 'London' excludes unknown cities because its result is unknown for them.
sections.code: SELECT id, city FROM customers WHERE city IS DISTINCT FROM 'London' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The single matching Retail customer is Cleo. This result says the email is absent; it does not prove why it is absent.

id | name
— | —
3 | Cleo

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: NULL = NULL is unknown, not true. NOT unknown stays unknown. An unmatched NOT IN test can also become unknown when its list contains NULL; use a correctly correlated NOT EXISTS when testing missing relationships.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: For Boolean expressions, true OR unknown is true, while false AND unknown is false. For duplicate removal and GROUP BY, NULLs are grouped together under different rules from ordinary equality.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Consider missing values explicitly in every filter. Compare IS NULL, <> and IS DISTINCT FROM on the same data, and explain which unknown rows each includes.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: NULL records missing information. Test it with IS NULL, and remember that WHERE discards unknown results as well as false ones.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: LIKE matches text against a simple pattern. % matches any sequence, including no characters; _ matches exactly one character. ILIKE performs case-insensitive matching using the applicable locale rules.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Patterns help find names beginning with a prefix or containing a fragment without needing a separate query for every possible name.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A LIKE pattern describes the whole string. 'Notebook%' matches a Notebook prefix; '%book%' matches that fragment anywhere. An escape character makes % or _ ordinary text rather than wildcards.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: name LIKE 'Notebook%' tests the product name. The percent sign permits any ending, including no ending. ORDER BY id sorts matching products; it is unrelated to pattern matching.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'Notebook%' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example matches Notebook and would also match Notebook Mini. It does not match a name containing Notebook only in the middle.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'Notebook%' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: In LIKE '%!_%' ESCAPE '!', the first and last % allow surrounding text, while !_ means a literal underscore. This finds an underscore anywhere in a customer name.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%!_%' ESCAPE '!' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Only Notebook matches the prefix in Retail. The additional dataset includes another matching name, so the rule must match prefixes rather than one hardcoded product.

id | name
— | —
1 | Notebook

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: LIKE wildcards differ from regular expressions: . and * are not its wildcard operators. A pattern starting with % often prevents an ordinary B-tree prefix lookup. Matching NULL produces unknown.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: ILIKE is convenient when letter case should be ignored. PostgreSQL 18 LIKE also follows the chosen collation, which can affect comparisons; do not assume every database treats text identically.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test an exact prefix, extra ending characters, the fragment in the middle, and literal wildcard characters. State whether case should matter before choosing LIKE or ILIKE.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use % for any sequence, _ for one character, and ESCAPE for literal wildcards. Choose matching rules that fit the text and the user's intent.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A regular expression is a text pattern with rules for positions, groups of characters, and repetition. PostgreSQL supports POSIX-style expressions, with additional features, for matching and extracting text.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Simple prefixes often need only LIKE. Regular expressions help when a condition needs a character range, a repeated sequence, or extraction of a specific part of a value.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ~ tests for a case-sensitive match; ~* ignores case. ^ marks the start and $ the end. Without anchors, a pattern can match part of a string. [A-D] matches one character in that range.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: name ~ '^[A-D]' requires the first character to match A through D under the database's matching rules. It does not require the rest of the name to consist of those letters.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE name ~ '^[A-D]' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example returns customers whose names begin with A, B, C, or D in this dataset. Anchoring at the start prevents a later letter from being enough.
sections.code: SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE name ~ '^[A-D]' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: substring(email FROM '^[^@]+') extracts consecutive characters from the start up to the first @. Inside brackets, ^ negates the character set; + means one or more. It extracts text, rather than validating a full email address.
sections.code: SELECT id, substring(email FROM '^[^@]+') AS username FROM customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Ada, Ben, Cleo, and Davi match the small example in Retail. The result remains sorted by ID, independently of the pattern.

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada
2 | Ben
3 | Cleo
4 | Davi

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: An unanchored pattern does not validate the entire string. A character range can depend on collation, and complicated expressions can consume substantial time. Use a simple, bounded pattern when possible.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: LIKE has only a few wildcard rules; regular expressions offer richer matching. Extraction can return NULL when no match exists, which is separate from filtering out a row.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Read each pattern one symbol at a time. Check the difference between ^ outside and inside brackets, and test a value that matches only in the middle.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use anchors for positions, brackets for character choices, and repetition symbols deliberately. Distinguish testing a match from extracting text and from validating an entire value.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: CASE chooses an output value according to conditions. It does not remove rows or update a table; it is an expression that can be used wherever a value is needed.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reports often need labels such as low stock or customer priority. CASE keeps those rules visible in the query instead of storing labels that may become outdated.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A searched CASE tests WHEN conditions in order and uses the first true condition's THEN value. ELSE supplies a fallback; without ELSE, the fallback is NULL. All possible result values need compatible types.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: CASE starts the expression. WHEN stock = 0 THEN 'empty' handles zero first. WHEN stock < 10 THEN 'low' handles remaining low stock. ELSE 'ready' handles the rest; END closes CASE.
sections.code: SELECT id, CASE WHEN stock = 0 THEN 'empty' WHEN stock < 10 THEN 'low' ELSE 'ready' END AS stock_status FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: A stock value of zero also satisfies stock < 10. Putting the zero test first ensures it receives empty rather than low.
sections.code: SELECT id, CASE WHEN stock = 0 THEN 'empty' WHEN stock < 10 THEN 'low' ELSE 'ready' END AS stock_status FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The customer example gives VIP customers priority 1 before considering London for priority 2. Thus a VIP customer in London still receives 1. The result is sorted by priority, then ID.
sections.code: SELECT id, CASE WHEN vip THEN 1 WHEN city = 'London' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END AS priority FROM customers ORDER BY priority, id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Retail's Monitor and Lamp are low, Mug is empty, and the other products are ready. Each product still contributes one row.

id | stock_status
— | —
1 | ready
2 | ready
3 | ready
4 | low
5 | empty
6 | low
7 | ready
8 | ready

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A broad condition placed first can hide a more specific one. NULL conditions do not count as true. CASE usually evaluates only the chosen branch, but it cannot guarantee protection from every planning-time error.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: WHERE decides which rows remain; CASE chooses a value. Another form, CASE expression WHEN value THEN ... END, compares one expression with alternatives using equality. It does not match NULL with WHEN NULL; use a searched CASE with IS NULL.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test boundary values such as 0, 9, and 10, then check a row matching two WHEN conditions. Explain why the first match is the right one.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: CASE returns the first matching branch's value. Order conditions carefully, choose a meaningful fallback, and keep result types compatible.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: COALESCE returns the first argument that is not NULL. NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a and b compare equal; otherwise it returns a.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: These expressions make fallback text and safer calculations readable. They also let a report keep the distinction between a missing value and a real zero.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') uses city when present; COALESCE returns NULL if every argument is NULL. NULLIF(denominator, 0) turns zero into NULL, so division returns NULL rather than an error. Compatible argument types are required.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: SELECT id identifies the customer. COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') calculates city_label for display. It does not write Unknown into the stored city column.
sections.code: SELECT id, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city_label FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example preserves known cities and displays Unknown only for missing ones. An empty city string remains empty because it is not NULL.
sections.code: SELECT id, COALESCE(city, 'Unknown') AS city_label FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: COALESCE(email, name) uses the email when present and the name otherwise. Argument order expresses preference; it is not a comparison of which string looks more complete.
sections.code: SELECT id, COALESCE(email,name) AS contact FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Eli's city_label is Unknown in Retail, while the other city names are unchanged. The source city is still NULL for Eli.

id | city_label
— | —
1 | London
2 | Paris
3 | London
4 | Berlin
5 | Unknown
6 | Paris

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Replacing an unknown number with zero can change totals and averages. NULLIF prevents zero division, but does not fix integer division: cast an operand if you need a fractional result.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: COALESCE is a concise alternative to a CASE checking for NULL. NULLIF creates a missing value for a particular comparison; IS NULL tests whether a value is already missing.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check known values, NULL, and empty strings separately. For a ratio, decide what a zero denominator means before choosing whether to leave NULL or show a fallback.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use COALESCE to choose a meaningful fallback and NULLIF to suppress a particular value such as zero. Neither should hide missing information without a reason.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A data type determines how a value is stored and what operations mean. A cast converts a value to another type when a supported conversion exists. NUMERIC represents decimal values without binary floating-point approximation.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A ratio needs fractions; money often needs controlled decimal precision. Choosing types deliberately prevents a calculation from losing information before it is displayed.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CAST(value AS type) and value::type request the same conversion. With integer operands, division truncates toward zero. Converting an operand to numeric before division gives decimal arithmetic.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: 5::numeric converts 5 first, then / 2 calculates the ratio. AS ratio names the result. Casting the result of 5 / 2 afterward would be too late to recover the lost fraction.
sections.code: SELECT 5::numeric / 2 AS ratio;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example produces 2.5, displayed with extra decimal places by PostgreSQL's numeric formatting. Those trailing zeros do not change its mathematical value.
sections.code: SELECT 5::numeric / 2 AS ratio;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: occurred_at::date keeps the calendar date and removes the time-of-day from each event timestamp. With timestamps that include time zones, the selected date can also depend on the session time zone.
sections.code: SELECT id, occurred_at::date AS event_date FROM events ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The displayed ratio is 2.5000000000000000. A different number of trailing zeros does not mean the division has produced a different value.

ratio
—
2.5000000000000000

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A cast can fail on invalid text or an out-of-range value. For example, NUMERIC(10,2) rounds to two decimal places and allows eight digits before the decimal point; exceeding that capacity raises an error. Floating-point numbers are approximate.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Casting changes the value's type; round changes numerical precision for a calculation or display. Date conversion is another kind of information reduction, so consider what you are discarding.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Before calculating, identify each operand's type. Compare integer and decimal division, and test values that require rounding or do not fit a target type.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose the type before the operation that needs it. Casts can change precision or discard detail, and invalid conversions produce errors rather than guessed values.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An aggregate summarizes several rows in one value. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(expression) counts rows where that expression is not NULL. COUNT(DISTINCT expression) counts different non-NULL values.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Counting customers, known addresses, and represented cities answers three different questions. Choosing the right form makes the reported metric match its description.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Without GROUP BY, COUNT summarizes all rows left after WHERE and returns one row. For no input rows, COUNT returns 0; common aggregates such as SUM and AVG return NULL instead.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: count(*) counts every customers row, regardless of missing columns. AS customer_count supplies the heading. There is no GROUP BY because the whole table is one summary.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) AS customer_count FROM customers;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example asks how many customers exist, not how many have a known city or email. Each row contributes exactly once.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) AS customer_count FROM customers;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: count(DISTINCT city) reports the number of different known cities. Repeated London entries count once, and missing cities do not count at all.
sections.code: SELECT count(DISTINCT city) AS city_count FROM customers;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Retail has six customer rows, so customer_count is 6. A NULL in one of their columns does not stop COUNT(*) counting that row.

customer_count
—
6

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: COUNT(city) is not a customer count when city can be NULL. COUNT(1) counts a non-NULL constant for every row, so it behaves like COUNT(*), not like counting a special column.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: GROUP BY, introduced later, produces one count per group. With a LEFT JOIN, count of a non-NULL right-side key counts matches; COUNT(*) also counts the placeholder for an unmatched left row.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: State what one counted unit means before choosing syntax. Compare row count, known-value count, and distinct-value count, including a query whose filter matches no rows.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(column) skips NULL values, and COUNT(DISTINCT column) also removes repeated known values. Pick the form matching the question.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: SUM adds values, AVG finds their arithmetic mean, and MIN and MAX return the smallest and largest values. These aggregates ignore NULL inputs.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A price or inventory summary turns many rows into a few useful measurements. Give each measurement a name and units so a reader knows what it represents.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: WHERE first determines the input rows. Without GROUP BY, the aggregates then return one summary row. AVG divides by the number of non-NULL inputs, not by all rows. With no non-NULL inputs, these aggregates return NULL.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: min(price) and max(price) find price extremes; avg(price) calculates the mean. round(..., 2) rounds that numeric average to two decimal places. AS assigns clear headings to all three results.
sections.code: SELECT min(price) AS minimum_price, max(price) AS maximum_price, round(avg(price),2) AS average_price FROM products;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small example describes the price distribution without returning a row for each product. Rounding changes the displayed average, not the stored prices.
sections.code: SELECT min(price) AS minimum_price, max(price) AS maximum_price, round(avg(price),2) AS average_price FROM products;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: sum(price * stock) adds the stock value calculated for each product. sum(stock) counts the available units. One is a monetary amount; the other is a quantity, so their units differ.
sections.code: SELECT sum(price * stock) AS inventory_value, sum(stock) AS unit_count FROM products;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Retail's minimum price is 2.00, maximum is 250.00, and mean rounded to two decimals is 51.44. All three values share one output row.

minimum_price | maximum_price | average_price
— | — | —
2.00 | 250.00 | 51.44

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: SUM(x) / COUNT(*) differs from AVG(x) when x contains NULL, and integer division may truncate. An unweighted average of group averages is wrong when groups have different sizes.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: COUNT measures how many inputs exist; SUM and AVG measure their values. Grouped reports use the same aggregates but calculate them separately for each group.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the units of every formula. Compare results with a missing value and with no matching rows; decide whether NULL or a deliberate fallback communicates the right meaning.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Aggregates summarize known values. Choose the correct input rows, keep units clear, and account for NULL and unequal group sizes when computing averages.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: FILTER restricts the rows used by one aggregate. Several aggregates in the same query can therefore summarize different subsets of a shared input.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A report can show paid and pending order counts side by side without separate queries or a complicated join between summaries.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Write aggregate(...) FILTER (WHERE condition). Only true conditions pass that aggregate's filter. An outer WHERE still removes rows for every aggregate, so use it only for restrictions shared by all metrics.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') counts paid orders. The pending_count expression has its own condition. Both read orders, and neither filter removes rows from the other's calculation.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid_count, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') AS pending_count FROM orders;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The result has one paid count and one pending count. Cancelled orders contribute to neither, but remain in the source table.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid_count, count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') AS pending_count FROM orders;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: SUM(CASE WHEN vip THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) adds one for each VIP customer and zero for others. The second expression does the corresponding calculation for non-VIP customers.
sections.code: SELECT sum(CASE WHEN vip THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS vip_count, sum(CASE WHEN NOT vip THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS other_count FROM customers;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Retail contains nine paid and two pending orders. The remaining cancelled order is not included in either count.

paid_count | pending_count
— | —
9 | 2

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: COUNT(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts both 1 and 0 because neither is NULL. SUM without an ELSE can return NULL when no rows match; COUNT with FILTER returns zero.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: FILTER and CASE can express similar conditional summaries, but their NULL and empty-input behavior must match the intended metric. SUM with ELSE 0 still returns NULL when the entire input is empty.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: For every metric, name exactly which rows contribute. Test no matching rows and an entirely empty input before deciding whether a missing total should display as zero.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use FILTER for a condition local to one aggregate. Keep shared WHERE restrictions separate and check COUNT versus SUM behavior on empty inputs.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: GROUP BY puts rows with the same grouping values together. An aggregate then summarizes each group, producing one output row per group rather than per source row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A report may need one row per category or department. Grouping changes the level of detail from individual items to the groups that answer that question.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Choose grouping columns first, then calculate aggregates over each group's rows. NULL grouping values belong to one group. Selected columns generally must be grouped or aggregated; a grouped primary key can also determine its table's other columns.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: GROUP BY category forms one group per category. count(*) counts its products. SELECT category identifies the group, while ORDER BY category controls the final order separately.
sections.code: SELECT category, count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example counts products in each category. Two products sharing a category increase its count rather than create separate output rows.
sections.code: SELECT category, count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The employee example groups by department, counts people, and averages their salaries. Each output row describes a department, not one employee.
sections.code: SELECT department, count(*) AS employee_count, round(avg(salary),2) AS average_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department ORDER BY department;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Retail has two Home, three Office, and three Tech products. These group counts add up to the eight product rows.

category | product_count
— | —
Home | 2
Office | 3
Tech | 3

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Adding id to GROUP BY changes the level to individual products. GROUP BY does not guarantee sorted output. Do not select an arbitrary ungrouped value from a group containing several possible values.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: WHERE chooses input rows before grouping. HAVING, introduced next, chooses groups after aggregates have been calculated. DISTINCT removes repeats without calculating group summaries.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: HAVING filters groups after their aggregates are calculated. WHERE filters individual source rows before they are grouped, so the two clauses answer different questions.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A report may need categories with at least three products or customers whose total paid spending exceeds a threshold. Those decisions depend on a completed summary.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use WHERE for eligible input rows, GROUP BY for the grouping keys, and HAVING for conditions on the resulting group. Only groups with a true HAVING condition remain.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: GROUP BY category counts each category. HAVING count(*) >= 3 keeps groups with three or more products. ORDER BY category sorts those surviving groups.
sections.code: SELECT category, count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING count(*) >= 3 ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Home has only two products and is excluded. Office and Tech each have three, so both satisfy the inclusive threshold.
sections.code: SELECT category, count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING count(*) >= 3 ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The spending example first keeps paid orders with known customers. It then sums each customer's totals and uses HAVING sum(total) > 100 to select customers exceeding 100.
sections.code: SELECT customer_id, sum(total) AS spend FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id HAVING sum(total) > 100 ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The small example returns Office and Tech, each with product_count = 3. It removes a category group, not selected products within that category.

category | product_count
— | —
Office | 3
Tech | 3

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: WHERE total > 100 keeps individual large orders; HAVING sum(total) > 100 tests combined spending. A SELECT alias such as spend is not available in HAVING in the same query; repeat its aggregate.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A query with aggregates and HAVING can also operate without explicit GROUP BY, treating the whole input as one group. For ordinary group reports, choose clear grouping keys first.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Separate each task into a row eligibility rule and a group eligibility rule. Check whether a boundary is strict or inclusive and consider several small rows that meet a combined threshold.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: WHERE selects rows; GROUP BY forms summaries; HAVING selects those summaries. Put each condition at the level where its meaning belongs.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Grouping sets calculate several summaries from the same input. ROLLUP builds hierarchical subtotals; CUBE builds all combinations of grouping columns; GROUPING SETS lists exactly the combinations you want.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A report can show category totals and an overall total together. One query keeps their filters and measures consistent instead of repeating similar summary queries.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ROLLUP(a,b) requests (a,b), (a), and (). CUBE(a,b) adds (b) as well. The empty set () means one overall group. Omitted grouping columns display NULL, so GROUPING identifies whether a NULL marks a subtotal.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: ROLLUP(category) requests each category and the overall total. sum(stock) calculates units. grouping(category) is 0 for category rows and 1 for the total; ORDER BY is_total, category puts totals last.
sections.code: SELECT category, sum(stock) AS units, grouping(category) AS is_total FROM products GROUP BY ROLLUP(category) ORDER BY is_total, category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small example adds a single overall row after the category rows. The same stock values contribute both to their category's total and to the overall total.
sections.code: SELECT category, sum(stock) AS units, grouping(category) AS is_total FROM products GROUP BY ROLLUP(category) ORDER BY is_total, category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The employee CUBE reports department/manager pairs, departments alone, managers alone, and all employees. grouping(department, manager_id) records the omitted keys as a bit mask: 0 for both included, 1 for department only, 2 for manager only, 3 for neither.
sections.code: SELECT department, manager_id, count(*) AS headcount, grouping(department,manager_id) AS grouping_mask FROM employees GROUP BY CUBE(department,manager_id) ORDER BY grouping_mask, department NULLS LAST, manager_id NULLS LAST;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Category units are 8, 180, and 67; the overall total is 255. Its category is NULL and is_total is 1, distinguishing it from an actual missing category.

category | units | is_total
— | — | —
Home | 8 | 0
Office | 180 | 0
Tech | 67 | 0
NULL | 255 | 1

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Do not treat every NULL as an overall total: source data may contain real NULLs. CUBE doubles the number of grouping combinations for each additional column, so its result can grow rapidly.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: ROLLUP suits a hierarchy such as year/month; CUBE suits independent dimensions. GROUPING SETS lets you avoid subtotals that a report does not need.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Label the summary level before reading the figures. Compare each GROUPING mask with the columns omitted at that level, including genuine NULL values in the input.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose the grouping combinations a report needs and use GROUPING to label their levels. A subtotal's placeholder NULL is different from missing source data.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: INNER JOIN combines rows from two sources when its ON condition is true. Each matching pair becomes a result row; rows without a match are excluded.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Customer details and orders belong in separate tables, but reports need both. Joining their keys connects the information without storing copies of customer details in every order.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Use short aliases to identify each source. A join may produce zero, one, or several matches for an input row. A customer's several orders repeat that customer's details in the result.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: orders o and customers c give the tables aliases. ON c.id = o.customer_id matches each order's customer reference to a customer key. o.id AS order_id clarifies which ID is displayed.
sections.code: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, o.total FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small example attaches the customer's name to each order with a known customer. Guest orders with NULL customer_id do not match this equality and are absent.
sections.code: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, o.total FROM orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The inventory query joins each product_id to products.id, then multiplies inventory quantity by product price. The join supplies columns needed for the value calculation.
sections.code: SELECT i.product_id, p.name AS product, i.warehouse, i.quantity * p.price AS value FROM inventory i JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id ORDER BY i.product_id;

sections.body:
The full Retail result has eleven rows, with up to eight shown. The guest order is excluded; customers with several orders appear on several rows.

order_id | customer | total
— | — | —
101 | Ada | 29.00
102 | Ben | 75.00
103 | Ada | 250.00
104 | Cleo | 15.00
105 | Davi | 90.00
106 | Ben | 20.00
107 | Eli | 25.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Joining by a display name can create false matches if names repeat. An incomplete condition can multiply rows. Prefer explicit ON relationships and qualify columns shared by both sources.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: INNER JOIN keeps matching pairs. A LEFT JOIN, introduced next, also preserves left-side rows with no match. A foreign key protects references but does not automatically write the join condition for you.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace a result row back to its two source rows. Count matches for one customer and check why a guest order does not appear.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Join on the relationship that the data model defines. INNER JOIN returns every matching pair, so always consider both missing and multiple matches.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: LEFT JOIN preserves every left-side row. It returns matching pairs when present; if no right-side row matches, it supplies one result row with NULLs for the right-side columns.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A customer list should often include people with no orders. An inner join would lose them, while a left join keeps the customer visible.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ON decides which right rows match. A later WHERE condition can remove result rows, including the NULL-filled rows. To count matches, use a right-side column that cannot be NULL in a real matching row.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: customers c is the preserved side. LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id connects orders. ORDER BY c.id, o.id NULLS LAST groups each customer's output and specifies where missing order IDs appear.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, o.id AS order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY c.id, o.id NULLS LAST;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: A customer with several orders appears several times, once per order. A customer with none still appears once, with order_id shown as NULL.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, o.id AS order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY c.id, o.id NULLS LAST;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The paid-count example puts status = 'paid' in ON, preserving customers with no paid orders. count(o.id) then gives zero for those customers, because the missing right-side key is NULL.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, count(o.id) AS paid_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid' GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The full Retail result has twelve rows, with up to eight shown. Fara has no order and is retained with a NULL order_id; Ada contributes three actual order rows.

— | —
1 | 101
1 | 103
1 | 108
2 | 102
2 | 106
2 | 111
3 | 104

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: WHERE o.status = 'paid' after the join removes customers with no paid match. COUNT(*) counts the unmatched placeholder too, so it is unsuitable for counting actual orders in this pattern.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: LEFT JOIN answers 'include all left rows, optionally adding matches'. EXISTS answers whether a match exists without repeating left rows; the appropriate choice depends on the required output.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check a customer with no orders, one order, and several orders. Compare a right-side filter in ON with the same filter in WHERE before using an aggregate.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose the preserved side deliberately. Keep optional-match restrictions in ON and count a non-NULL right key when you need the number of real matches.

COUNT(*) counts the unmatched placeholder row. COUNT(right_table.id) counts only actual matches.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: RIGHT JOIN preserves every right-side row; FULL JOIN preserves unmatched rows on both sides. CROSS JOIN has a different job: it produces every possible pair of input rows.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Outer joins help compare two lists without losing unmatched entries. Cross joins help build combinations, such as every product category paired with every warehouse.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RIGHT JOIN is the mirror of LEFT JOIN. FULL JOIN adds NULLs for whichever side is absent. CROSS JOIN uses no ON condition: N left rows and M right rows produce N × M pairs, including zero if either source is empty.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: orders RIGHT JOIN customers preserves customers on the right. ON connects customer IDs; SELECT still chooses the output column order, independently of which source is preserved.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, o.id AS order_id FROM orders o RIGHT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id NULLS LAST;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small example is equivalent to starting with customers and using LEFT JOIN orders. Customers without orders remain, with a NULL order ID.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id, o.id AS order_id FROM orders o RIGHT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY c.id, o.id NULLS LAST;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The realistic example first gets distinct categories and distinct warehouses, then pairs them using CROSS JOIN. Deduplicating each input prevents repeated combinations caused by repeated source values.
sections.code: SELECT c.category, w.warehouse FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) c CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT warehouse FROM inventory) w ORDER BY c.category, w.warehouse;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The small Retail example has twelve rows, including the customer without orders. Up to eight are shown; their column order is set by SELECT, not by RIGHT JOIN.

customer_id | order_id
— | —
1 | 101
1 | 103
1 | 108
2 | 102
2 | 106

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A cross join can grow very quickly: 1,000 rows on each side mean 1,000,000 pairs. A WHERE condition rejecting NULLs from an outer join can discard rows you intended to preserve.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Swapping a RIGHT JOIN to LEFT JOIN can make a report easier to read. FULL JOIN is useful for reconciliation; CROSS JOIN is suitable only when every combination is actually wanted.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Draw which side must survive without a match. For a cross join, calculate the expected row count from the two input counts before running it.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Outer joins preserve unmatched data; cross joins enumerate combinations. Choose the join by the required rows and check how large its result can become.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A self join reads the same table under different aliases. Each alias plays a different role, allowing one row to be matched with another row from the same table.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Employees and managers have the same stored fields, so one employees table can describe both. A self join turns the stored manager reference into a readable manager name.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Treat employees e as the employee and employees m as the manager. Match e.manager_id to m.id. A LEFT JOIN preserves employees whose manager reference is NULL.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The FROM clause introduces e and the join introduces m. m.id = e.manager_id identifies the manager. e.name AS employee and m.name AS manager distinguish the two names in the output.
sections.code: SELECT e.id, e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id ORDER BY e.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Morgan has no manager and remains with a NULL manager name. Noor links to Morgan; Owen and Rae link to Noor. The query follows one manager link, not the whole hierarchy.
sections.code: SELECT e.id, e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id ORDER BY e.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: For employee pairs in a department, e1.id < e2.id excludes a person paired with themself and avoids listing both (A,B) and (B,A). Equality on department limits pairs to colleagues.
sections.code: SELECT e1.id AS first_id, e2.id AS second_id FROM employees e1 JOIN employees e2 ON e1.department = e2.department AND e1.id < e2.id ORDER BY first_id, second_id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
All six Retail employees appear. Morgan's NULL manager reflects a missing relationship, not an employee named NULL.

id | employee | manager
— | — | —
1 | Morgan | NULL
2 | Noor | Morgan
3 | Owen | Noor
4 | Pia | Morgan
5 | Quinn | Pia
6 | Rae | Noor

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: The aliases refer to the same stored table, not separate copies. Unqualified id or name is ambiguous. A foreign key can require a manager to exist without preventing every possible cycle in the hierarchy.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A self join follows a fixed number of links. Recursive CTEs, taught later, can follow an unknown number of levels; pair joins need a deliberate rule for whether direction and duplicates matter.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Label each alias's role before joining. Check a top-level employee, a subordinate, and colleague pairs, and explain why a pair should appear once or twice.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use distinct aliases for distinct roles in one table. Join the correct link, preserve missing relationships when required, and control self-pairs and mirrored pairs explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A join's cardinality is the number of matching result rows. Joining one order to several order lines repeats that order's columns once for each line. This repetition is expected, but it changes how totals must be calculated.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: An order total and a line total describe different units. A report can look plausible while counting the same order amount several times after a one-to-many join.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: First state what one result row represents: an order, an order line, or a customer. Connect each relationship by its keys. If a later join multiplies existing summaries, aggregate the many-side data before joining it.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: Orders o joins customers c by customer ID, order_items i by order ID, and products p by product ID. quantity * unit_price calculates each line's value; ORDER BY o.id, p.id gives line-key order.
sections.code: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, i.quantity, i.quantity * i.unit_price AS line_total FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id ORDER BY o.id, p.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Each output row describes one product line with a known customer. Order 101 appears twice because it contains Notebook and Pen; those are two legitimate lines, not accidental duplicates.
sections.code: SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, i.quantity, i.quantity * i.unit_price AS line_total FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id ORDER BY o.id, p.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The customer summary uses count(DISTINCT o.id) for orders and count(*) for lines. After joining order_items, an order with several lines must contribute once to order_count but several times to line_count.
sections.code: SELECT o.customer_id, count(DISTINCT o.id) AS order_count, count(*) AS line_count FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.customer_id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The full Retail result contains twelve known-customer lines, with up to eight shown. The first two lines belong to order 101 and have values 25.00 and 4.00.

order_id | customer | product | quantity | line_total
— | — | — | — | —
101 | Ada | Notebook | 2 | 25.00
101 | Ada | Pen | 2 | 4.00
102 | Ben | Keyboard | 1 | 75.00
103 | Ada | Monitor | 1 | 250.00
104 | Cleo | Mug | 1 | 15.00
105 | Davi | Lamp | 2 | 90.00
106 | Ben | Pen | 10 | 20.00
107 | Eli | Notebook | 2 | 25.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: SUM(o.total) after joining order lines repeats an order total per line. SUM(DISTINCT o.total) is also unsafe: different orders can have identical totals. Fix the level of aggregation, not just visible duplicates.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: JOIN combines related rows, GROUP BY changes the summary level, and EXISTS tests membership without multiplying outer rows. Choose the pattern that matches the intended unit of your report.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Write the unit of each metric beside its formula. Check an order with multiple lines and two orders with equal totals; both cases expose common overcounting mistakes.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Follow the keys and track what one row means after every join. Aggregate at the correct level so repeated detail rows do not inflate higher-level measures.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: EXISTS is true when its subquery returns at least one row. NOT EXISTS is true when it returns none. Both produce a definite true or false result, not an unknown result.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Questions such as 'has any order?' need one answer per customer, even when that customer has many orders. An existence test avoids multiplying output rows just to check a relationship.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A correlated subquery refers to an outer query alias. Its condition defines which rows count as matches. SELECT 1 conventionally signals that only row existence matters; NULL values in those rows do not make EXISTS unknown.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: For each customers c row, the subquery looks for orders o with o.customer_id = c.id. WHERE EXISTS keeps the customer if a match exists. The outer ORDER BY controls the displayed order.
sections.code: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Ada qualifies once even though several orders match. Fara has no order and is excluded. The test does not return the matching order columns.
sections.code: SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The product example uses NOT EXISTS with order_items joined to paid orders. A product qualifies only if no paid order contains it; appearing solely in cancelled orders does not disqualify it.
sections.code: SELECT p.id, p.name FROM products p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.id = i.order_id WHERE i.product_id = p.id AND o.status = 'paid') ORDER BY p.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Forgetting the correlation can make EXISTS depend on any order anywhere rather than that customer's orders. Nullable NOT IN results differ from NOT EXISTS; the predicates are not interchangeable without checking NULL behavior.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: EXISTS expresses a matching requirement, sometimes called a semi-join; NOT EXISTS expresses an absence requirement, or anti-join. These names describe row-selection behavior rather than extra SQL keywords you need to write here.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test zero, one, and several matching rows. Add a nonqualifying related row, such as a cancelled order, and check that the business condition remains inside the subquery.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use EXISTS for at least one qualifying match and NOT EXISTS for none. Make the correlation and the qualifying conditions explicit.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A scalar subquery supplies one value inside another expression. It must return one column and no more than one row. Zero rows give NULL; multiple rows cause an error.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A query often needs a calculated benchmark, such as the average price of all products. A subquery calculates that benchmark from current data rather than hardcoding a number.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Put the inner SELECT in parentheses where a value is expected. An aggregate without grouping usually supplies one summary row; its value may still be NULL if there are no qualifying inputs.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The inner SELECT avg(price) FROM products calculates one overall average. The outer WHERE compares each product's price with that value. ORDER BY id sorts the products that pass.
sections.code: SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products) ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example finds products priced above the overall average, rather than above a fixed threshold. Adding or changing a product can change that average and the qualifying rows.
sections.code: SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products) ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The stock-share example divides each product's stock by a scalar sum of all stock. Casting stock to numeric preserves fractions; NULLIF(..., 0) leaves the share unknown when the total is zero.
sections.code: SELECT id, round(stock::numeric / NULLIF((SELECT sum(stock) FROM products),0),4) AS stock_share FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Keyboard and Monitor are above the Retail average. The average itself is used for comparison and is not an extra displayed output column.

id | name | price
— | — | —
3 | Keyboard | 75.00
4 | Monitor | 250.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A filter returning one row today may return several tomorrow. Use a key or an appropriate aggregate when one row is required; adding LIMIT 1 without a meaningful rule can hide ambiguity.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A scalar subquery produces a value. A subquery in FROM produces a table, while EXISTS checks row presence. Choose the form matching what the surrounding query needs.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Identify the inner query's row and column counts before embedding it. Check no qualifying rows, a NULL aggregate result, and an unexpectedly duplicated lookup key.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A scalar subquery must provide at most one row and exactly one column. Account for NULL when no value is available, and make uniqueness intentional.
