sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A correlated subquery uses a value from an outer query row. Its question therefore depends on that row, such as 'what is the average price in this product's category?'

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Comparing every product with the overall average may hide category differences. A correlated calculation supplies a benchmark for the group to which each product belongs.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Give inner and outer sources different aliases. A reference to the outer alias links the inner condition to the current outer row. This describes the query's meaning; the execution plan determines whether work is repeated or transformed.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: products p is the outer product. Inside, products p2 supplies the comparison group, limited by p2.category = p.category. avg(p2.price) is that category's average; the outer price must exceed it.
sections.code: SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price FROM products p WHERE p.price > (SELECT avg(p2.price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category) ORDER BY p.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: A product is compared with its own category, including itself in that average. Office and Tech products are not pooled into one benchmark in this query.
sections.code: SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price FROM products p WHERE p.price > (SELECT avg(p2.price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category) ORDER BY p.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The customer example counts orders whose customer_id matches each outer customer ID. COUNT returns zero when no order matches, so customers without orders remain in the output.
sections.code: SELECT c.id, (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS order_count FROM customers c ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Notebook, Monitor, and Lamp exceed their own category averages in Retail. This differs from comparing all products with one overall average.

id | name | price
— | — | —
1 | Notebook | 12.50
4 | Monitor | 250.00
6 | Lamp | 45.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Omitting p2.category = p.category turns the benchmark into an overall average. Reusing aliases or leaving ambiguous references unqualified can accidentally change which source a column belongs to.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Correlation concerns dependency, not a particular execution speed. Joins or grouped summaries can express related calculations; compare plans and results before assuming one form is faster.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Write the outer row's question in words. Then point to the exact inner condition using its value, and test rows from different groups and rows with no related records.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A correlated subquery answers a row-specific question through an explicit outer reference. Clear aliases and a complete correlation condition protect its meaning.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A derived table is a query used as a source in FROM. LATERAL allows such a query to refer to sources on its left, making a related table result for each outer row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Separate query layers make a summary of summaries possible. LATERAL also expresses questions such as the two most expensive products in each category without mixing their limits together.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A FROM subquery can return many rows and columns; an alias names its output for the outer query. Unlike an ordinary independent subquery, a LATERAL subquery may use a preceding source's values.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The inner query counts orders per known customer. Its alias counts names that summary table. The outer avg(order_count) averages those counts, and round(..., 2) rounds the resulting average.
sections.code: SELECT round(avg(order_count),2) AS average_orders FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id) counts;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example averages orders among customers who have orders with non-NULL customer_id. It does not include customers with no orders as zero-count groups, because they are absent from this inner result.
sections.code: SELECT round(avg(order_count),2) AS average_orders FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id) counts;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The LATERAL example starts from distinct categories. For each category it sorts matching products by price descending, then ID, and takes at most two. The final ORDER BY arranges the combined output.
sections.code: SELECT c.category, p.id, p.price FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) c CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT id, price FROM products p WHERE p.category = c.category ORDER BY price DESC, id LIMIT 2) p ORDER BY c.category, p.price DESC, p.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The small Retail example returns average_orders = 2.20: eleven known-customer orders divided among five customers with orders. It is not an average across all six customers.

average_orders
—
2.20

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops an outer row if the inner query returns no rows. LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true preserves it with NULLs. Sorting inside a subquery does not establish the final output order.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A scalar subquery returns a single value; a derived table supplies rows and columns. LATERAL makes a table-producing subquery dependent on an earlier source, like correlation with a table-shaped result.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check who belongs to the inner summary before averaging it. For top-N queries, verify that LIMIT applies separately per category and that equal prices have a tie-breaker.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use a derived table to separate calculation stages. Use LATERAL for a related row set per outer row, choosing CROSS or LEFT behavior when matches are absent.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A common table expression, or CTE, gives a query result a name for use within one statement. WITH introduces these named stages before the main query.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Breaking a long calculation into named stages helps a reader follow where rows are filtered, grouped, and compared. The names describe the calculation rather than creating permanent tables.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Write WITH name AS (query), then use name as a source. Multiple CTEs are comma-separated and may read earlier CTEs. Their names last only for the current statement.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: WITH paid AS (...) defines a stage keeping paid order IDs and totals. The final SELECT reads paid, filters totals above 50, and sorts by ID. The inner and outer filters serve separate readable stages.
sections.code: WITH paid AS (SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid') SELECT id, total FROM paid WHERE total > 50 ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example separates the definition of a paid order from the later amount threshold. Its result is still the result of one SQL statement, not a stored table named paid.
sections.code: WITH paid AS (SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid') SELECT id, total FROM paid WHERE total > 50 ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: category_sales groups revenue from paid order lines by category. The final query compares each category's revenue with the mean of those category totals, reusing the named calculation.
sections.code: WITH category_sales AS (SELECT p.category, sum(i.quantity*i.unit_price) AS revenue FROM products p JOIN order_items i ON i.product_id=p.id JOIN orders o ON o.id=i.order_id WHERE o.status='paid' GROUP BY p.category) SELECT category, revenue FROM category_sales WHERE revenue > (SELECT avg(revenue) FROM category_sales) ORDER BY category;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Four Retail paid orders have totals above 50: IDs 102, 103, 105, and 111. The CTE name does not add another output column or result table.

id | total
— | —
102 | 75.00
103 | 250.00
105 | 90.00
111 | 75.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A CTE is not always an optimization barrier. PostgreSQL can fold a nonrecursive, side-effect-free SELECT CTE into its parent, commonly for a single use. MATERIALIZED can keep a separate calculation; NOT MATERIALIZED can allow folding when eligible.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A derived table gives a query layer an inline position; a CTE gives it a name before the main query. Neither automatically persists data. Recursive and data-changing CTEs have additional rules taught separately.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Name each stage by what it represents. Trace its columns and row filters, then verify that a later comparison uses totals at the intended level rather than raw rows.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use WITH to make query stages clear and reusable within one statement. Treat materialization as a planning choice, not an automatic property of every CTE.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: UNION stacks compatible query results and removes duplicate whole rows. UNION ALL also stacks results, but keeps every input row, including duplicates.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Data from separate sources can share one report format. Choosing ALL preserves repeated transactions that happen to have the same displayed values.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Both branches need the same number of columns with compatible types in corresponding positions. Columns match by position, not by name; output headings normally come from the first branch. Only a final ORDER BY guarantees combined ordering.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The first branch returns known customer cities as place; the second returns warehouses in the same column position. UNION removes repeated place values, and ORDER BY place sorts the combined list.
sections.code: SELECT city AS place FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL UNION SELECT warehouse FROM inventory ORDER BY place;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: London appears for several customers but appears once in the result. A warehouse name is included under the same place heading even though its source column has another name.
sections.code: SELECT city AS place FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL UNION SELECT warehouse FROM inventory ORDER BY place;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The business example combines paid order totals and booking charges under source and amount. UNION ALL keeps separate transactions even if their source labels and amounts happen to match.
sections.code: SELECT 'order' AS source, total AS amount FROM orders WHERE status='paid' UNION ALL SELECT 'booking', (check_out-check_in)*nightly_rate FROM bookings ORDER BY source, amount;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The Retail place list contains Berlin, London, North, Paris, and South. Its order comes from the final ORDER BY, not the order of query branches.

place
—
Berlin
London
North
Paris
South

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: UNION is not a join: it adds rows rather than attaching columns. Dropping ALL can silently discard valid repeated transactions. NULLs count as equal for duplicate removal; UNION ALL preserves them as separate rows.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Use JOIN for related columns on the same row and UNION for similarly shaped rows from different queries. Branch-specific ORDER BY or LIMIT needs parentheses when combined with a set operation.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Compare column positions and types before combining queries. Check two identical transactions and decide whether the business question wants both retained or just one distinct row.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: UNION combines rows and removes duplicates; UNION ALL preserves multiplicity. Define a shared column contract and sort the final result explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: INTERSECT returns rows found in both query results. EXCEPT returns rows found in the first result but absent from the second. By default, both remove duplicate whole rows.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: These operations express overlap and difference directly: customers with two kinds of orders, or products that appear in lines but never in paid orders.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Branches must have matching column counts and compatible corresponding types. INTERSECT ALL keeps the smaller duplicate count from the two sides; EXCEPT ALL subtracts the second count from the first, never below zero.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The two branches select non-NULL customer IDs from paid and pending orders. INTERSECT keeps IDs present in both. ORDER BY customer_id sorts the final overlap.
sections.code: SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status='paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status='pending' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: A customer qualifies by having at least one order of each status. The query does not require one order to have both statuses at once.
sections.code: SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status='paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status='pending' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The product example subtracts IDs appearing in paid order lines from all IDs appearing in order_items. A product with even one paid occurrence is absent from the difference.
sections.code: SELECT product_id FROM order_items EXCEPT SELECT i.product_id FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.id=i.order_id WHERE o.status='paid' ORDER BY product_id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Customer IDs 2 and 4 appear in both Retail status groups. Repeated orders do not repeat those IDs in the default INTERSECT result.

customer_id
—
2
4

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: EXCEPT is directional: reversing its branches changes the question. NULLs count as equal for set comparisons. INTERSECT binds more tightly than UNION or EXCEPT; parentheses make a mixed expression's meaning explicit.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: NOT EXISTS can express related absence questions while retaining other outer columns. A nullable NOT IN has different NULL behavior, so it is not a direct substitute for set difference.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Describe each branch's set before combining it. Check repeated rows, NULL, and one ID appearing on only one side, then verify whether ALL is appropriate.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: INTERSECT finds common rows; EXCEPT finds a directional difference. Choose duplicate handling and parentheses deliberately, and sort the final result when order matters.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: INSERT adds new rows to a table. RETURNING produces a result from the rows actually inserted, making their stored values available immediately to the caller.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: An application needs to know what was saved, including generated identifiers and defaults. RETURNING avoids guessing those values or issuing an unrelated lookup afterward.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Name the target columns, then supply corresponding VALUES in the same order. Omitted columns use their defaults, or NULL when no default exists; all constraints must still pass. INSERT ... SELECT inserts rows produced by a query.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: INSERT INTO products(...) identifies the table and five target columns. VALUES(...) supplies one product in that order. RETURNING id, name, price, stock chooses which inserted values to display.
sections.code: INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES (50,'Ruler','Office',3.50,15) RETURNING id,name,price,stock;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example inserts Ruler with ID 50, category Office, price 3.50, and stock 15. Other omitted columns use their defaults. RETURNING shows just that new row's requested fields.
sections.code: INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES (50,'Ruler','Office',3.50,15) RETURNING id,name,price,stock;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The archive example creates paid_archive with an order primary key, then copies paid order IDs and totals using INSERT ... SELECT. It copies values, not a live link to the orders table.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE paid_archive(order_id integer PRIMARY KEY,total numeric(10,2)); INSERT INTO paid_archive SELECT id,total FROM orders WHERE status='paid';

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Mismatched column/value positions can put data in the wrong place or raise a type error. Duplicate keys and other constraint violations fail unless specifically handled. A successful preview does not make exercise changes permanent outside its isolated run.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: INSERT changes rows; SELECT normally reads them. RETURNING turns changed rows into output. Upserts later add conflict-handling rules, while transactions determine whether a group of changes is committed together.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check both the returned row and the resulting table state. Confirm omitted-column defaults and constraint behavior, and remember that each practice execution starts from its controlled dataset.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: List INSERT columns explicitly, match values by position, and use RETURNING for saved values. Verify actual table changes separately from command output.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: UPDATE changes values in existing rows. It keeps the rows and changes only the columns listed in SET.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Use it to adjust stock, correct a price, or move an order to its next status.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: WHERE chooses the rows; SET calculates their new values from their previous values. RETURNING can show the changed rows without a separate SELECT.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: UPDATE products selects the table. SET stock=10 assigns a value. WHERE stock=0 limits the change to products currently out of stock.
sections.code: UPDATE products SET stock=10 WHERE stock=0;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Only zero-stock products receive 10 units. Products with any other stock value stay unchanged.
sections.code: UPDATE products SET stock=10 WHERE stock=0;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: UPDATE ... FROM matches each product to inventory by product_id, then uses quantity+2 as the new stock. The source must supply at most one matching row per product.
sections.code: UPDATE products p SET stock=i.quantity+2 FROM inventory i WHERE i.product_id=p.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The table below checks stored values after the small example; UPDATE itself does not return this table. Product 5 changes to 10, while other stock values remain the same.

id | stock
— | —
1 | 40
2 | 120
3 | 12
4 | 5
5 | 10
6 | 8
7 | 50
8 | 20

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Without WHERE, UPDATE changes every row. With multiple source matches in UPDATE ... FROM, the chosen source row is unpredictable. First inspect the intended rows with SELECT.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: JOIN explains how source rows match. Constraints still apply during UPDATE, and a transaction lets several related changes succeed together.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check both changed and unchanged products. Confirm that a second source match cannot accidentally choose a different quantity.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose rows carefully, calculate new values, then verify the resulting data.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: DELETE removes rows from a table. A foreign key can prevent deletion of a row that other rows still reference.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Removing old or unwanted data must leave relationships between the remaining rows valid.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DELETE FROM names the table and WHERE selects rows to remove. USING can supply related tables. TRUNCATE empties whole tables without a row condition, using different locks and triggers.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The subquery looks for an order with o.customer_id=c.id. NOT EXISTS is true only when no such order exists, so DELETE removes only customers without orders.
sections.code: DELETE FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Fara has no orders in the Retail dataset and is removed. A customer with even one order is kept.
sections.code: DELETE FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: TRUNCATE events removes every event but preserves the table definition. It does not run row-level DELETE triggers; it can run TRUNCATE triggers.
sections.code: TRUNCATE events;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
This checker table lists the five customers remaining after deletion. It is a separate read of the changed data, not direct DELETE output.

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada
2 | Ben
3 | Cleo
4 | Davi
5 | Eli

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Omitting WHERE deletes all rows. Referencing rows may block DELETE unless a foreign-key action allows it. PostgreSQL can roll back TRUNCATE, but it takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. Unlike DELETE, it can make a table appear empty to a concurrent transaction using an older snapshot.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: NOT EXISTS expresses an absence test. Foreign-key actions such as CASCADE or SET NULL define what happens to dependent rows.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Before deleting, run the same condition with SELECT. Check that customers with orders remain and that the resulting relationships are valid.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: DELETE chooses rows to remove; TRUNCATE empties tables. Understand dependencies before either operation.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An upsert tries to insert a row and handles a specified uniqueness conflict instead of simply failing.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: It helps imports and synchronisation jobs decide what to do when an identifier already exists.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ON CONFLICT ... DO NOTHING skips a conflicting insert. DO UPDATE changes the existing row. EXCLUDED names the proposed new values; the target table name refers to existing values.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: ON CONFLICT(product_id) uses the unique product key. Each SET assignment copies a proposed value from EXCLUDED into the existing inventory row.
sections.code: INSERT INTO inventory VALUES (1,'Central',60,DATE '2024-08-01') ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET warehouse=EXCLUDED.warehouse,quantity=EXCLUDED.quantity,updated_on=EXCLUDED.updated_on;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Product 1 already has an inventory row, so its warehouse, quantity, and date are replaced. If the key were absent, the proposed row would be inserted.
sections.code: INSERT INTO inventory VALUES (1,'Central',60,DATE '2024-08-01') ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET warehouse=EXCLUDED.warehouse,quantity=EXCLUDED.quantity,updated_on=EXCLUDED.updated_on;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The second example adds EXCLUDED.quantity to the existing quantity. It changes the date but deliberately keeps the existing warehouse.
sections.code: INSERT INTO inventory VALUES(2,'North',5,DATE '2024-08-01') ON CONFLICT(product_id) DO UPDATE SET quantity=inventory.quantity+EXCLUDED.quantity,updated_on=EXCLUDED.updated_on;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
This table checks stored inventory after the first example. Product 1 becomes Central, 60, and 2024-08-01; the other rows remain unchanged.

product_id | warehouse | quantity | updated_on
— | — | — | —
1 | Central | 60 | 2024-08-01
2 | North | 120 | 2024-07-01
3 | South | 12 | 2024-07-02
4 | South | 5 | 2024-07-02
5 | North | 0 | 2024-07-03
6 | South | 8 | 2024-07-03
7 | North | 50 | 2024-07-04
8 | North | 20 | 2024-07-04

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: DO UPDATE needs a suitable non-deferrable unique key or index; exclusion constraints cannot be its conflict target. Other errors still fail. Repeating an additive upsert adds again, so not every upsert is safe to retry unchanged.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A primary key is a common conflict target. Compare replacement with accumulation: both use upsert, but their business meaning differs.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test the existing-key and missing-key cases. Read each assignment and decide whether it replaces, preserves, or adds to a value.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose the conflict key and merge rule explicitly; EXCLUDED contains the attempted insert.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A transaction groups changes into one unit: commit all of them or discard them. A savepoint marks a place inside that unit to return to.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A bank transfer must not debit one account without crediting the other.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BEGIN opens a transaction. COMMIT keeps its changes; ROLLBACK cancels them. SAVEPOINT names an intermediate point, and ROLLBACK TO undoes later work while keeping the transaction open.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The first UPDATE subtracts 100 from account 1; the second adds 100 to account 2. BEGIN and COMMIT place both updates in one transaction.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The transfer changes balances to 900 and 600 while keeping their combined amount unchanged.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The savepoint follows the first addition of 10. Rolling back to it cancels only the later addition of 100, so committing preserves the first addition.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+10 WHERE id=1; SAVEPOINT before_extra; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+100 WHERE id=1; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_extra; COMMIT;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The table checks balances after the completed transfer. The UPDATE commands do not directly return these rows.

id | balance
— | —
1 | 900.00
2 | 600.00
3 | 750.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: After a statement error, the transaction normally refuses further work until rollback. Rolling back to a suitable earlier savepoint can recover it. Atomicity alone does not validate missing account IDs or every concurrent business rule.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Constraints reject invalid balances. Isolation and row locks address concurrent transactions; those are separate from grouping statements atomically.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check both balances and their sum. Trace exactly which changes survive a savepoint rollback. Each practice execution starts with a fresh isolated dataset.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Transactions control what is kept; savepoints allow a partial undo before the final commit.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A data-changing CTE puts INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE inside WITH. Its RETURNING rows can feed the rest of the same SQL statement.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: This connects a change to a report or follow-up insert without passing changed rows through application code.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A modifying CTE executes once and completes even if its output is not fully read. Its RETURNING output, not a fresh read of the target table, communicates changes to other parts of the statement.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: WITH changed AS (...) names the UPDATE output. RETURNING id,price exposes the new prices, and the final SELECT reads and sorts those rows.
sections.code: WITH changed AS (UPDATE products SET price=price-1 WHERE category='Home' RETURNING id,price) SELECT id,price FROM changed ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Home products lose 1 from their price. The direct SELECT output contains only the changed products.
sections.code: WITH changed AS (UPDATE products SET price=price-1 WHERE category='Home' RETURNING id,price) SELECT id,price FROM changed ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The added CTE inserts Eraser and returns its id and name. The final SELECT reads that output as a small result table.
sections.code: WITH added AS (INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES(51,'Eraser','Office',1.25,30) RETURNING id,name) SELECT id,name FROM added;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The table below is the dedicated state check for all products after the small example. It differs from the statement's direct output, which lists only changed rows.

id | price
— | —
1 | 12.50
2 | 2.00
3 | 75.00
4 | 250.00
5 | 14.00
6 | 44.00
7 | 8.00
8 | 4.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Sibling modifying CTEs share a snapshot; their physical order is not a reliable communication mechanism. Use RETURNING dependencies and avoid changing the same row twice in one statement.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Ordinary CTEs organise queries; modifying CTEs also have effects. A transaction can group several statements when one WITH statement is unnecessary.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Distinguish returned changed rows from a later whole-table check. Verify both the new values and the rows that must stay unchanged.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use RETURNING as the explicit data flow between a modification and its consumer.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A data type tells PostgreSQL what a value means and which operations it supports: numbers, text, or true/false values.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: The right type prevents invalid values and avoids surprising comparisons or calculations.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: smallint, integer, and bigint store exact whole numbers in different ranges. numeric stores decimal values precisely within its declared limits; real and double precision are approximate. text stores characters; boolean stores true or false, with NULL allowed unless prohibited.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: pg_typeof(value) reports a value's type. The ::text casts make those type names ordinary text columns, and AS names the outputs.
sections.code: SELECT pg_typeof(1)::text AS integer_type, pg_typeof(1.5)::text AS decimal_type, pg_typeof('x'::text)::text AS text_type, pg_typeof(true)::text AS boolean_type;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: PostgreSQL interprets 1 as integer, 1.5 as numeric, 'x'::text as text, and true as boolean.
sections.code: SELECT pg_typeof(1)::text AS integer_type, pg_typeof(1.5)::text AS decimal_type, pg_typeof('x'::text)::text AS text_type, pg_typeof(true)::text AS boolean_type;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The expression 'product-' || id::text combines a text prefix with the product ID converted to text.
sections.code: SELECT id, 'product-' || id::text AS label FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The single result row contains type names, not the original values. A column's type and the way its value is displayed are different things.

integer_type | decimal_type | text_type | boolean_type
— | — | — | —
integer | numeric | text | boolean

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: numeric(p,s) limits precision and scale and may round input. varchar(n) limits characters, not bytes. Text 'true' is not itself a boolean, even though an explicit conversion can produce one.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Casts convert values between compatible types. Constraints express additional rules such as positive quantities or required text.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Read the type as well as the displayed value. Check whether a calculation requires exact decimals, an integer range, or text formatting.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose types for meaning and valid operations; use explicit casts where conversion is needed.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A UUID is a 128-bit identifier. An enum is a named type that accepts only a declared set of text labels.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: UUIDs help create identifiers across systems. Enums restrict a column to a small, deliberately maintained set of states.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A known UUID can be cast from text. PostgreSQL 18 offers uuidv4() for random UUIDs and uuidv7() for time-ordered UUIDs. CREATE TYPE ... AS ENUM declares labels and their comparison order.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The quoted value is UUID text; ::uuid validates and converts it. AS identifier gives the result column its name.
sections.code: SELECT '123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000'::uuid AS identifier;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example returns a fixed UUID so that repeated runs produce the same value.
sections.code: SELECT '123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000'::uuid AS identifier;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: request_log uses a UUID primary key and a required note. Inserting a known identifier illustrates storage without depending on random generation.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE request_log(request_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,note text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO request_log VALUES('00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001','imported');

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
One UUID value appears under identifier. The displayed hyphens are formatting; the stored type is uuid rather than text.

identifier
—
123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Enum labels are case-sensitive and sort in declaration order, not alphabetically. Removing labels requires more work than adding them. A UUID does not by itself enforce a table key; declare PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare an enum with a CHECK constraint or a lookup table. A lookup table is often easier when states need their own editable metadata.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Keep fixed identifiers in reproducible exercises. Check that an enum accepts only declared labels and that its ordering matches the intended rule.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use UUIDs for identifiers and enums for carefully chosen finite states; their roles are different.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: String functions inspect or transform text. Here, normalisation means applying the same cleanup rules before comparing or storing values.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Extra spaces and inconsistent letter case often make equivalent input look different.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: lower and upper change case; trim removes surrounding spaces by default. length counts characters. concat_ws joins non-NULL arguments with a separator. Most text transformations return a value without changing stored data.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: lower(email) produces lowercase text. WHERE email IS NOT NULL excludes missing addresses; AS normalized_email names the computed column.
sections.code: SELECT id, lower(email) AS normalized_email FROM customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The query displays known email addresses in lowercase, ordered by customer ID. It does not update customers.
sections.code: SELECT id, lower(email) AS normalized_email FROM customers WHERE email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: length(name) produces name_length. Descending length puts longer names first; id resolves ties consistently.
sections.code: SELECT id,name,length(name) AS name_length FROM customers ORDER BY name_length DESC,id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The shown emails already use lowercase, so their appearance stays the same. Cleo is absent because her email is NULL.

id | normalized_email
— | —
1 | ada@example.test
2 | ben@example.test
4 | davi@example.test
5 | eli@example.test
6 | fara@example.test

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: length counts characters; octet_length counts bytes. trim does not remove all possible internal whitespace. Case conversion depends on locale and is not a universal rule for all identifiers or email systems.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: This text cleanup differs from relational normalisation, which concerns table design. Expression indexes can support frequently used text transformations.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test missing text, leading spaces, and equal-length names. Decide whether you want a transformed result or an UPDATE of stored data.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose a clear cleanup rule and apply it consistently; know whether it changes output or storage.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: DATE stores a calendar day without a time of day. Date arithmetic can count days or move to another calendar date.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Bookings, deadlines, and follow-up dates need clear rules about which days are included.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Subtracting one date from another returns an integer number of days. Adding an integer to a date moves by that many days. Write DATE '2024-07-01' to make a date literal unambiguous.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: check_out-check_in computes nights for each booking. AS nights labels the result; ORDER BY id gives a stable display order.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest,check_out-check_in AS nights FROM bookings ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: A stay from July 1 to July 4 lasts three nights: July 1, 2, and 3. Checkout day is not an occupied night.
sections.code: SELECT id,guest,check_out-check_in AS nights FROM bookings ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: For pending orders, ordered_on+7 gives a follow-up date one week later. The query returns dates without changing the order rows.
sections.code: SELECT id,ordered_on+7 AS follow_up_on FROM orders WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The five displayed bookings have 3, 3, 2, 1, and 3 nights. These are whole-day differences, not elapsed timestamp hours.

id | guest | nights
— | — | —
1 | Ada | 3
2 | Ben | 3
3 | Cleo | 2
4 | Davi | 1
5 | Eli | 3

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A calendar month is not a fixed number of days. DATE subtraction differs from age(), which expresses calendar years, months, and days. Be explicit about inclusive and exclusive boundaries.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Timestamps add time of day and time-zone questions. Half-open ranges help represent stays whose checkout day is excluded.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check a one-night stay and a month boundary. Verify that adjoining stays can share a checkout/check-in date without overlapping nights.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: DATE arithmetic works with calendar days; state the boundary rule before calculating.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: timestamp without time zone stores calendar and clock fields. timestamptz identifies an instant; its displayed clock time depends on the session time zone.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A local appointment and a globally timed event need different treatment, even if their text looks similar.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For a timestamp without a zone, AT TIME ZONE interprets the clock fields in the named zone and produces timestamptz. For timestamptz, it produces local clock fields in that zone. The original zone name is not stored in timestamptz.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: EXTRACT(HOUR FROM occurred_at) reads the hour field; ::integer converts it to an integer. This does not convert time zones.
sections.code: SELECT id,EXTRACT(HOUR FROM occurred_at)::integer AS event_hour FROM events ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The events column is timestamp without time zone. The small example reads its stored hours directly.
sections.code: SELECT id,EXTRACT(HOUR FROM occurred_at)::integer AS event_hour FROM events ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The first AT TIME ZONE treats occurred_at as UTC. The second displays that instant as Tokyo local time, returning a timestamp without time zone.
sections.code: SELECT id,(occurred_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Tokyo' AS tokyo_time FROM events ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The event_hour values are 9, 9, 10, 8, 10, and 11. These are stored clock hours, not inferred UTC instants.

id | event_hour
— | —
1 | 9
2 | 9
3 | 10
4 | 8
5 | 10
6 | 11

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Do not assume a zone-less timestamp means UTC. Daylight-saving transitions can make a local time ambiguous or nonexistent. Explicit offsets or a clear input policy avoid guessing.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: DATE contains no time of day. Reporting with timestamptz also needs a chosen zone before extracting dates or grouping days.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace the type after each AT TIME ZONE. Check a conversion that crosses midnight, not only one that changes the hour.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: First identify whether you have clock fields or an instant, then apply the intended zone.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An interval expresses a span using months, days, and smaller time units. date_trunc finds the start of a calendar period containing a timestamp.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reports need consistent month boundaries; elapsed-time calculations need a clear starting point and unit.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: date_trunc('month', value) clears the smaller date/time fields. Timestamp subtraction produces an interval; EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM interval) expresses it in seconds. Calendar units do not all have a fixed number of seconds.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: date_trunc groups each ordered_on into its month. ::date displays the month start as a date; sum(total) adds the rows in each group.
sections.code: SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The monthly summary includes every order status because the query has no status filter. It is a sum of order totals, not automatically a paid-revenue report.
sections.code: SELECT date_trunc('month',ordered_on)::date AS month_start,sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY month_start ORDER BY month_start;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Subtracting the fixed midnight timestamp gives the time since that start. Dividing extracted seconds by 60 expresses the interval in minutes.
sections.code: SELECT id,EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (occurred_at-TIMESTAMP '2024-07-01 00:00:00'))/60 AS minutes_since_start FROM events ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The three month-start rows show totals 369, 151, and 374 on Retail. The query's explicit ORDER BY puts the months in sequence.

month_start | revenue
— | —
2024-05-01 | 369.00
2024-06-01 | 151.00
2024-07-01 | 374.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A month has varying length, and a local day across daylight-saving changes may not be 24 hours. now() stays at transaction-start time; clock_timestamp() changes as time passes. Choose the reporting zone for timestamptz.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An array stores an ordered collection whose elements share a type, such as several text tags on one product.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Arrays suit small values that belong together. A separate relationship table is often better when elements need their own keys or references.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ARRAY[...] constructs an array. value = ANY(array) compares with its elements. @> tests containment; cardinality counts elements; unnest turns elements into rows. Array indexes usually start at 1 but can have other lower bounds.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: 'usb'=ANY(tags) asks whether any tag equals usb. WHERE keeps matching products, and ORDER BY id sorts the result.
sections.code: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE 'usb'=ANY(tags) ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Keyboard and Cable contain the usb tag in Retail, so they are returned.
sections.code: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE 'usb'=ANY(tags) ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: LATERAL unnest(p.tags) produces one row per tag for each product. GROUP BY tag then counts those expanded rows.
sections.code: SELECT t.tag,count(*) AS product_count FROM products p CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(p.tags) AS t(tag) GROUP BY t.tag ORDER BY product_count DESC,t.tag;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The small example returns products 3 and 7. Membership tests keep product rows; they do not return one row for every tag.

id | name
— | —
3 | Keyboard
7 | Cable

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: An empty array differs from a NULL array. If no comparison is true but an element is NULL, = ANY may be unknown. Repeated tags count repeatedly after unnest; the product_count example assumes unique tags within each product.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare unnest with a one-to-many join: both can increase row count. Containment ignores repeated occurrences, unlike an expanded count.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check empty arrays, NULLs, and duplicate tags. Decide whether you are counting tag occurrences or distinct products.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Arrays keep collections together; unnest expands them, so track the resulting row count.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: json stores JSON text. jsonb stores a processed representation suited to structural operations and indexes. Both can hold objects, arrays, and scalar values.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: JSON is useful for variable optional attributes, while regular columns remain useful for stable shared fields and constraints.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: -> keeps the extracted value as JSON; ->> returns text. #>> follows a path and returns text. Missing keys return SQL NULL. Convert extracted text to numeric before doing numeric arithmetic.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: attributes->>'color' reads color as text. AS color names the output; no WHERE filter removes products with missing color.
sections.code: SELECT id,attributes->>'color' AS color FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Every product appears. A missing color gives SQL NULL rather than removing the row.
sections.code: SELECT id,attributes->>'color' AS color FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: For purchase events, the query extracts device and converts amount to numeric before summing by device.
sections.code: SELECT payload->>'device' AS device,sum((payload->>'amount')::numeric) AS amount FROM events WHERE kind='purchase' GROUP BY device ORDER BY device;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Monitor, Cable, and Folder have NULL color in the displayed Retail result. Those missing values are different from the text 'NULL'.

id | color
— | —
1 | blue
2 | black
3 | black
4 | NULL
5 | white
6 | blue
7 | NULL
8 | NULL

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: JSON null and SQL NULL differ, although ->> returns SQL NULL for either a missing key or JSON null. jsonb keeps only the last duplicate object key and does not preserve formatting or key order. A numeric cast fails on nonnumeric text.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: JSONB containment checks structure without extracting every field. Constraints and relational columns can protect fields that must always be valid.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check absent keys, JSON null, and numeric strings. Inspect whether an operator returns JSON or text before combining it with other operations.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose the extraction operator by the result type you need, and convert numeric text explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: JSONB can be searched by structure and transformed into a new document. These operations work on values; storing the new document requires a write such as UPDATE.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: You can filter optional attributes or change one field while keeping the rest of a document.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: @> tests whether a document contains the given JSON structure. ? tests a top-level key or string array element. jsonb_set takes a document, a text-array path, a JSONB value, and an optional create-missing flag.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The right operand '{"color":"blue"}'::jsonb is an object. @> matches documents containing that color even if they also contain other keys.
sections.code: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"color":"blue"}'::jsonb ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Notebook and Lamp have color blue in Retail; extra attributes do not stop the match.
sections.code: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"color":"blue"}'::jsonb ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: UPDATE stores jsonb_set's returned document for Office products. '{featured}' is the path; 'true'::jsonb is a Boolean JSON value, not a text string.
sections.code: UPDATE products SET attributes=jsonb_set(attributes,'{featured}','true'::jsonb,true) WHERE category='Office';

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The small example returns products 1 and 6. This is a structural containment match, not a search for the word blue anywhere in JSON text.

id | name
— | —
1 | Notebook
6 | Lamp

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: JSON number 2 differs from JSON string "2". A missing intermediate path is not built automatically by jsonb_set; only the final item can be created when its parents exist. Updating the document replaces the stored value, so keep the original as the function's input.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Use ->> when you need a text value, @> when you need a structural match. Important relationships may still belong in relational columns.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check that only Office documents change and that unrelated keys survive. Distinguish JSON true from the JSON string "true".

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Match JSON structure deliberately, then store the transformed document when an actual change is needed.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Keys protect identity and relationships. PRIMARY KEY identifies a row uniquely and forbids NULL; UNIQUE prevents repeated key values; FOREIGN KEY requires a referenced row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Database-enforced keys keep data consistent regardless of which application writes it.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE can cover one or several columns. A foreign key can reference a suitable unique key. A nullable single-column foreign key permits NULL without a parent match; use NOT NULL to make the relationship required.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: customer_notes.id is the primary key. customer_id is required and references customers(id); body is required text. The insert links a note to customer 1.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_notes(id integer PRIMARY KEY,customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),body text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO customer_notes VALUES(1,1,'Call after 5');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The note belongs to an existing customer. A different note needs a new id, but several notes may share customer_id.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_notes(id integer PRIMARY KEY,customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),body text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO customer_notes VALUES(1,1,'Call after 5');

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: customer_alias uses UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT on alias. Unlike ordinary UNIQUE, this rule allows at most one NULL alias.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_alias(customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id),alias text UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker lists column types and nullability after table creation. It is metadata output from a separate query; key correctness also depends on the declared constraints.

column_name | data_type | is_nullable
— | — | —
id | integer | NO
customer_id | integer | NO
body | text | NO

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Ordinary UNIQUE allows multiple NULLs. A foreign key does not automatically index the referencing column. By default, any NULL in a foreign key with several columns skips the match. MATCH FULL allows all key columns to be NULL together and rejects a mix of NULL and present values.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A primary key identifies the note, while a foreign key identifies its relationship. An index helps access data; a constraint states a rule.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Inspect keys as well as columns. Try reasoning about duplicate IDs, missing customers, and NULL aliases before submitting a table design.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Separate row identity, uniqueness rules, and required relationships; declare each one explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: CHECK rejects a row when a condition is false. DEFAULT supplies an omitted value. A foreign-key action says what to do when a referenced row changes or is deleted.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: These rules keep ordinary writes simple while protecting required business conditions.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CHECK accepts true or unknown, so use NOT NULL as well when missing values are invalid. DEFAULT applies when a column is omitted or DEFAULT is requested, not when NULL is explicitly supplied. CASCADE propagates a parent change; SET NULL clears a reference.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: quantity has default 1, forbids NULL, and must be greater than zero. Inserting only id lets PostgreSQL supply the quantity.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE reservations(id integer PRIMARY KEY,quantity integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK(quantity>0)); INSERT INTO reservations(id) VALUES(1);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The new reservation receives quantity 1. Supplying zero would violate CHECK; supplying NULL would violate NOT NULL.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE reservations(id integer PRIMARY KEY,quantity integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK(quantity>0)); INSERT INTO reservations(id) VALUES(1);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Adding promoted with NOT NULL DEFAULT false gives existing products false and supplies false for future inserts that omit the column.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN promoted boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker reads the created reservation and shows id 1 with quantity 1. CREATE TABLE itself does not return this data table.

id | quantity
— | —
1 | 1

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Changing an existing column's default does not rewrite its old values. This differs from adding a new column with a default. CHECK is not a safe way to maintain rules that depend on other rows. Cascading deletes can remove many dependent rows.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Foreign keys handle relationships; CHECK handles conditions on a row. Defaults provide values but do not replace validation.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check omitted, explicit NULL, and invalid values separately. For a referential action, trace exactly which dependent rows will change.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use defaults for convenience and constraints for validity; keep their roles separate.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An identity column gets values from an associated sequence, an object that hands out numbers. Generation and uniqueness are separate rules.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Automatic IDs avoid making every insert choose a new number manually.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY normally rejects an explicit ID; BY DEFAULT permits one. Identity implies NOT NULL, but a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint must enforce uniqueness. RETURNING can retrieve generated IDs.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: activity_log has an identity primary key and required message. The insert names only message, so the sequence supplies the IDs.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE activity_log(id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,message text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO activity_log(message) VALUES('Started'),('Finished');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: On the fresh table, Started and Finished receive IDs 1 and 2.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE activity_log(id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,message text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO activity_log(message) VALUES('Started'),('Finished');

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: BY DEFAULT allows the explicit legacy ID 50. That insert does not advance the sequence to 50, so the following generated ID on this fresh table is 1.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE imported_log(id integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,message text); INSERT INTO imported_log VALUES(50,'Legacy'); INSERT INTO imported_log(message) VALUES('New');

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker shows the two saved messages and generated IDs. The creation and insert statements do not directly produce this table.

id | message
— | —
1 | Started
2 | Finished

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Sequence numbers are not reclaimed after rollback and can have gaps. Manual IDs do not automatically keep a sequence ahead of existing rows. An ID is neither a row count nor a guaranteed commit-time order.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: UUIDs offer another identifier strategy. Primary keys protect identity regardless of how values are generated.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Distinguish ALWAYS from BY DEFAULT. Check what a manual insert does to the next generated value and whether uniqueness is enforced.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A sequence generates numbers; a key makes them unique. Expect gaps.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Normalisation organises data so that each property is stored with the entity it describes. A relationship table links two entities when each can relate to many of the other.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Keeping one authoritative copy of a property reduces inconsistent updates and accidental data loss.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Identify entities and keys, then ask which key determines each property. In a many-to-many relationship table, the pair of foreign keys often forms a primary key, preventing the same link from being stored twice.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: favorites links a customer and a product. Each column references its parent table; PRIMARY KEY(customer_id,product_id) makes the pair unique and both parts required.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE favorites(customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id),product_id integer REFERENCES products(id),PRIMARY KEY(customer_id,product_id)); INSERT INTO favorites VALUES(1,3),(2,1);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The inserted links mean customer 1 likes product 3 and customer 2 likes product 1. Neither product details nor customer names are copied.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE favorites(customer_id integer REFERENCES customers(id),product_id integer REFERENCES products(id),PRIMARY KEY(customer_id,product_id)); INSERT INTO favorites VALUES(1,3),(2,1);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The categories example extracts distinct category names and assigns deterministic IDs in alphabetical order. It creates a lookup table; it does not yet replace products.category with a foreign key.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE categories(id integer PRIMARY KEY,name text NOT NULL UNIQUE); INSERT INTO categories SELECT row_number() OVER(ORDER BY category)::integer,category FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) c;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker shows the two saved customer/product links. The table's key prevents duplicate pairs, while each individual ID may appear in several different pairs.

customer_id | product_id
— | —
1 | 3
2 | 1

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Normalisation does not mean making a table for every column. Splitting a design without preserving keys and dependencies can lose meaning. Denormalise only with a clear consistency strategy and a measured need.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Primary and foreign keys make relationships enforceable. JOIN combines normalised tables when a report needs their properties together.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: For each new table, state what one row represents and what identifies it. Check whether repeated text is a property or a relationship.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Store each property in the right place and represent many-to-many links explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A schema is a named container for database objects. Catalogs are database tables and views describing objects such as tables, columns, and constraints.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Schemas organise names; metadata queries let tools inspect a database without hardcoding every table definition.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A qualified name such as schema.table identifies the schema explicitly. Otherwise search_path supplies a list to search. information_schema provides standard metadata views; pg_catalog exposes PostgreSQL-specific details.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The columns view is filtered by current_schema() and table_name='customers'. ordinal_position orders the output by the table's declared column order.
sections.code: SELECT column_name,data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema=current_schema() AND table_name='customers' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The query describes customers; it does not read customer records. column_name and data_type are metadata fields.
sections.code: SELECT column_name,data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema=current_schema() AND table_name='customers' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Filtering information_schema.tables to BASE TABLE excludes views. The current-schema condition avoids mixing similarly named objects in other schemas.
sections.code: SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=current_schema() AND table_type='BASE TABLE' ORDER BY table_name;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The result lists id, name, city, email, joined_on, and vip with their types. Metadata visibility can depend on the current role's privileges.

column_name | data_type
— | —
id | integer
name | text
city | text
email | text
joined_on | date
vip | boolean

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A schema is not a separate database. current_schema() is the first effective schema in search_path, not every searched schema. Letting untrusted users create objects in a searched schema can change name resolution.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: The schema browser uses similar metadata. Roles and search_path matter for secure functions and administrative tooling.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Distinguish table data from metadata. Always check schema filters when a table name could exist in several places.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Qualify object names when needed, and use catalogs to inspect the database definition.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A migration is a recorded, repeatable change to database structure or data. It should leave both existing data and application expectations consistent.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Applications evolve while real data must survive. An ordered migration is safer to verify than ad hoc edits.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A common sequence is: add a column that permits NULL, fill existing rows, then enforce the new constraint. Many PostgreSQL schema commands can roll back in a transaction, but locks and command-specific restrictions still matter.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: ADD COLUMN creates segment. UPDATE fills it using vip. ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL is last, after every existing row has a value.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN segment text; UPDATE customers SET segment=CASE WHEN vip THEN 'priority' ELSE 'standard' END; ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN segment SET NOT NULL;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: VIP customers receive priority; all others receive standard. The final constraint prevents future missing segments.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN segment text; UPDATE customers SET segment=CASE WHEN vip THEN 'priority' ELSE 'standard' END; ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN segment SET NOT NULL;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: Adding reviewed_at without a default leaves existing orders NULL. This represents an unknown or not-yet-recorded review time.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN reviewed_at timestamp without time zone;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker shows segment values after all three steps. It is a separate read of the migrated data, not ALTER TABLE output.

id | segment
— | —
1 | priority
2 | standard
3 | standard
4 | priority
5 | standard
6 | standard

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Adding NOT NULL before filling NULL rows fails. This example does not set a future default, so later inserts must supply segment. Large tables may need staged backfills, lock planning, and compatible application deployment.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Defaults, constraints, and transactions each solve part of migration safety. Backups and restore tests protect against changes that cannot simply be reversed.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Verify old rows and the final schema. Ask what a new insert must provide after the migration, not just whether today's rows look correct.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Plan the order of change, backfill existing data, and check the rules for future writes.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A window function calculates using related rows while retaining each individual result row. This lets a detail row carry a group total beside it.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Reports often need both an employee's salary and the total for that employee's department.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OVER turns an aggregate into a window calculation. PARTITION BY separates rows into groups for that calculation. With no window ORDER BY, sum sees the whole partition. Without PARTITION BY, all input rows form one partition.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: sum(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department) totals salaries independently within each department. The outer ORDER BY id controls the displayed rows.
sections.code: SELECT id,department,salary,sum(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department) AS department_total FROM employees ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Engineering employees keep their own salaries and each show the same department total, 250000, on Retail.
sections.code: SELECT id,department,salary,sum(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department) AS department_total FROM employees ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: count(*) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id) repeats the customer's order count on each order. NULL customer IDs form their own partition rather than disappearing.
sections.code: SELECT id,customer_id,count(*) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_order_count FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Six employee rows remain. Department totals repeat because a window adds a calculation instead of collapsing the department to one row.

id | department | salary | department_total
— | — | — | —
1 | Leadership | 120000.00 | 120000.00
2 | Engineering | 90000.00 | 250000.00
3 | Engineering | 80000.00 | 250000.00
4 | Sales | 70000.00 | 140000.00
5 | Sales | 70000.00 | 140000.00
6 | Engineering | 80000.00 | 250000.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: GROUP BY changes result row granularity; a window does not do that grouping. WHERE and HAVING filter before window calculations. To filter by a window result, calculate it in a subquery or CTE first.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Ordinary aggregates produce summaries; window aggregates attach summaries to detail. A window ORDER BY, introduced next, can also change the calculation's frame.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Compare input and output row counts. Check that every department has its own total and that NULL partition keys are handled deliberately.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: PARTITION BY chooses related rows; OVER keeps the detail rows while calculating across them.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: row_number assigns a different number to each ordered row. rank gives tied rows the same rank and leaves gaps; dense_rank gives ties the same rank without gaps.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Use these functions for leaderboards, ordered positions, and selecting a limited number of rows within each group.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The ORDER BY inside OVER defines ranking order. Rows equal on every window sort expression are peers. For values 100, 100, 80, rank gives 1,1,3 and dense_rank gives 1,1,2; row_number gives 1,2,3.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: PARTITION BY category starts numbering again for each category. ORDER BY price DESC,id places expensive products first and resolves equal prices by ID.
sections.code: SELECT id,category,row_number() OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS position FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The output is displayed by id, so position need not increase down the visible table. It reflects the separate ordering inside each category.
sections.code: SELECT id,category,row_number() OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS position FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The CTE first numbers employees within departments, then rn<=2 keeps at most two from each. The ID tie-breaker chooses a consistent result when salaries match.
sections.code: WITH ranked AS (SELECT *,row_number() OVER(PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC,id) AS rn FROM employees) SELECT id,name,department,salary FROM ranked WHERE rn<=2 ORDER BY department,salary DESC,id;

sections.title: Expected results

— | — | —
1 | Office | 1
2 | Office | 3
3 | Tech | 2
4 | Tech | 1
5 | Home | 2
6 | Home | 1
7 | Tech | 3
8 | Office | 2

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: The outer ORDER BY does not define window order. Adding id to rank removes salary ties. Decide whether 'top two' means exactly two rows or every row in the top two ranks.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A subquery or CTE lets WHERE filter a computed window value. DISTINCT ON is another option when only one row per group is needed.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test equal salaries. Compare which employees survive row_number<=2 versus rank<=2 before choosing the function.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose numbering for a row limit and ranking for meaningful ties; define the window order explicitly.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: lag reads a value from an earlier row in the window's order; lead reads one from a later row. Neither requires a self join.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Compare successive orders, salaries, or events while retaining each current row.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The default offset is one row. An optional third argument supplies a default only when that row does not exist. PostgreSQL does not skip NULL values. Partition boundaries stop the lookup.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: PARTITION BY customer_id keeps customers separate. ORDER BY ordered_on,id defines which order precedes another. lag(total) returns that preceding row's total.
sections.code: SELECT id,customer_id,total,lag(total) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id) AS previous_total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Ada's order 103 sees 29 from order 101; her order 108 sees 250 from order 103. Each customer's first order gets NULL.
sections.code: SELECT id,customer_id,total,lag(total) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id) AS previous_total FROM orders ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The salary example subtracts the preceding employee's salary in hire-date order within the same department. It compares employees, not salary history for one employee.
sections.code: SELECT id,salary-lag(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department ORDER BY hired_on,id) AS salary_change FROM employees ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
NULL previous_total marks a first row in these data. More generally, it can also mean that a preceding row exists but its total is NULL. The displayed preview may show only part of the result.

id | customer_id | total | previous_total
— | — | — | —
101 | 1 | 29.00 | NULL
102 | 2 | 75.00 | NULL
103 | 1 | 250.00 | 29.00
104 | 3 | 15.00 | NULL
105 | 4 | 90.00 | NULL
106 | 2 | 20.00 | 75.00
107 | 5 | 25.00 | NULL
108 | 1 | 16.00 | 250.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A default argument does not replace a NULL in an existing neighbouring row. Date ties need a tie-breaker. The final display order can differ from the order used by lag or lead.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Window partitions define independent sequences. A self join can express similar comparisons but often needs more key-handling code.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace one customer's orders by window order. Check the first row, equal dates, and a neighbour whose value is missing.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define the sequence first; lag and lead then read neighbours inside that sequence.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A window frame is the portion of a partition used for the current calculation. It can grow with each row to produce a running total.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Running revenue answers 'how much so far?' without losing individual orders.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ROWS counts positions in the window order. RANGE uses ordering values and peer groups; GROUPS counts peer groups. UNBOUNDED PRECEDING starts at the partition's first row, and CURRENT ROW ends at the current position in ROWS mode.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: WHERE keeps paid orders before the window calculation. ORDER BY ordered_on,id defines a unique sequence; the explicit ROWS frame sums from its beginning through the current order.
sections.code: SELECT id,ordered_on,sum(total) OVER(ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' ORDER BY ordered_on,id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The first paid order contributes 29; adding the next 75 gives 104. Cancelled and pending orders do not contribute.
sections.code: SELECT id,ordered_on,sum(total) OVER(ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' ORDER BY ordered_on,id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: PARTITION BY customer_id restarts accumulation for each known customer. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING is shorthand for a frame ending at the current row.
sections.code: SELECT id,customer_id,sum(total) OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_spend FROM orders WHERE status='paid' AND customer_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The preview shows increasing paid-order totals in date/ID order. It may stop before the last row, so its last visible total need not be the complete total.

id | ordered_on | running_revenue
— | — | —
101 | 2024-05-01 | 29.00
102 | 2024-05-02 | 104.00
103 | 2024-05-10 | 354.00
105 | 2024-06-01 | 444.00
107 | 2024-06-05 | 469.00
108 | 2024-06-10 | 485.00
110 | 2024-07-03 | 530.00
111 | 2024-07-04 | 605.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: With an ordered window, the default RANGE frame includes all peers at the current sort value. A total can jump across equal dates. Use an explicit frame and a tie-breaker when row-by-row steps matter.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A whole-partition sum repeats one total; a running sum uses a changing frame. The outer ORDER BY still controls how the result is displayed.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test same-day orders and two customers. Check that filtering happens before summing and that a new partition starts again.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Specify partition, order, and frame to make a running calculation unambiguous.
