sections.title: The idea
sections.body: first_value and last_value read the first and last value of the current window frame. ntile splits an ordered partition into numbered groups of rows.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: These functions compare rows with a chosen endpoint or divide a ranked list into roughly equal-sized groups.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The frame matters for endpoint functions. To read the final value of a whole partition, end the frame at UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. ntile(n) balances row counts; earlier buckets receive extra rows when the division is uneven.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: first_value(price) reads the first price in each category's descending price order. With this ordering, the first price is the category maximum.
sections.code: SELECT id,first_value(price) OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS category_max FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Every Office product shows 12.50 as category_max on Retail, while every Tech product shows 250.00.
sections.code: SELECT id,first_value(price) OVER(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC,id) AS category_max FROM products ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: ntile(4) divides all six employees in salary/ID order into four buckets. The buckets have 2, 2, 1, and 1 rows on this dataset.
sections.code: SELECT id,ntile(4) OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC,id) AS quartile FROM employees ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: The default ordered frame usually ends at the current peer group, so last_value may not mean 'last in the partition'. ntile divides rows, not value ranges, and can split equal salaries into different buckets. NULLs are not skipped.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: max() OVER can express a whole-partition maximum directly. Ranking and bucketing differ: rank preserves ties, while ntile aims for balanced row counts.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Endpoint functions follow the frame; ntile balances ordered rows, not numeric intervals.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: DISTINCT ON is a PostgreSQL feature that keeps one representative row for each group of key values. The ordering decides which row wins.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: It is a compact way to select a latest event or highest-priced item per group while keeping that row's other columns.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The DISTINCT ON keys must match the leftmost ORDER BY expressions. Later sort expressions choose the first row within each group. Without a complete tie-breaking rule, the choice can vary.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: DISTINCT ON(customer_id) keeps one order per customer. customer_id leads ORDER BY, then descending date chooses the latest order and descending id resolves date ties.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT ON(customer_id) customer_id,id AS order_id,ordered_on FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY customer_id,ordered_on DESC,id DESC;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The WHERE condition excludes anonymous orders. The query keeps the latest order of any status, including pending or cancelled orders.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT ON(customer_id) customer_id,id AS order_id,ordered_on FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY customer_id,ordered_on DESC,id DESC;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The event example applies the same rule to occurred_at, using the highest event ID to break identical timestamps.
sections.code: SELECT DISTINCT ON(customer_id) customer_id,id AS event_id,occurred_at FROM events ORDER BY customer_id,occurred_at DESC,id DESC;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The Retail result includes customer 4's pending order 109 because it is that customer's latest order. This is not a latest-paid-order query.

customer_id | order_id | ordered_on
— | — | —
1 | 108 | 2024-06-10
2 | 111 | 2024-07-04
3 | 110 | 2024-07-03
4 | 109 | 2024-07-01
5 | 107 | 2024-06-05

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: DISTINCT removes duplicate whole output rows; DISTINCT ON selects one row per key. To display chosen rows in a different overall order, wrap the selection in another query. PostgreSQL groups NULL keys together unless you filter them out.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: row_number with a filter can express a similar rule in more SQL systems. Both approaches need an explicit definition of 'first'.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check equal dates, different statuses, and NULL customers. Make sure the selected row matches the intended business rule.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Name the group keys, define the winning row, and keep the ORDER BY prefix compatible.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A view is a stored query definition that you can query by name. An ordinary view stores the definition, not a separate copy of its result rows.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A shared view keeps a reporting rule in one place instead of repeating it in every query.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE VIEW name AS query defines the view. Selecting from it reads the underlying data according to that query. Some simple views are writable; grouped or joined views are generally not automatically writable.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: paid_orders names a SELECT of four order columns filtered to status='paid'. Later queries can use FROM paid_orders.
sections.code: CREATE VIEW paid_orders AS SELECT id,customer_id,ordered_on,total FROM orders WHERE status='paid';

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The view exposes paid orders only. Creating it does not copy or remove rows in orders.
sections.code: CREATE VIEW paid_orders AS SELECT id,customer_id,ordered_on,total FROM orders WHERE status='paid';

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: customer_spending starts from every customer. The paid-status condition stays in the LEFT JOIN, and COALESCE changes a missing sum to zero, preserving customers without paid orders.
sections.code: CREATE VIEW customer_spending AS SELECT c.id AS customer_id,COALESCE(sum(o.total),0) AS paid_spend FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker reads the created paid_orders view. It may show only the first part of the result; callers must specify ORDER BY when order matters.

id | customer_id | ordered_on | total
— | — | — | —
101 | 1 | 2024-05-01 | 29.00
102 | 2 | 2024-05-02 | 75.00
103 | 1 | 2024-05-10 | 250.00
105 | 4 | 2024-06-01 | 90.00
107 | 5 | 2024-06-05 | 25.00
108 | 1 | 2024-06-10 | 16.00
110 | 3 | 2024-07-03 | 45.00
111 | 2 | 2024-07-04 | 75.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A view does not inherently make its query faster or guarantee a caller's row order. Privileges and row-security behavior depend on how the view is defined; do not assume it is automatically a security boundary.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A CTE names a query within one statement. A materialized view stores results and needs refresh; an ordinary view reads current underlying data under the query's snapshot.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check view columns and filters. For customer totals, confirm that customers with no paid orders remain and receive zero.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use views to reuse a query definition, and specify ordering and permissions deliberately.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A materialized view saves the rows produced by a query. Its contents stay as saved until an explicit refresh recomputes them.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A stored summary can make repeated reads cheaper when slightly old results are acceptable.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW normally runs the defining query and stores its result. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW replaces those rows. CONCURRENTLY allows reads during refresh, with additional requirements.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The SELECT groups products by category and sums stock. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW stores those groups under category_snapshot.
sections.code: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW category_snapshot AS SELECT category,sum(stock) AS stock_units FROM products GROUP BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The saved summary has one row per category. Later changes to products do not automatically change these saved totals.
sections.code: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW category_snapshot AS SELECT category,sum(stock) AS stock_units FROM products GROUP BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: customer_totals is initially populated, then receives a unique customer_id index. That full, column-only unique index makes the concurrent refresh eligible.
sections.code: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW customer_totals AS SELECT customer_id,sum(total) AS total FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id; CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customer_totals_key ON customer_totals(customer_id); REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY customer_totals;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker reads category_snapshot: Home has 8 units, Office 180, and Tech 67 on Retail. Creation itself does not return that table.

category | stock_units
— | —
Home | 8
Office | 180
Tech | 67

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A concurrent refresh requires an already populated view and a unique index on ordinary columns covering all rows. The index must use columns directly, without expressions or a WHERE clause. Only one refresh may run per materialized view at a time.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: An ordinary view reads its sources on demand; a materialized view trades freshness and storage for reusable results. Indexes can also support reads of the stored summary.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Ask when the summary was last refreshed. Check the defining query, refresh requirements, and whether callers can tolerate old results.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: A materialized view is a saved result, so plan both its reads and its refresh schedule.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A set-returning function produces rows rather than one scalar value. generate_series creates a sequence of numbers or times that can serve as a query's data source.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Generated calendars let reports include days with no recorded events and expand stays into individual nights.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: generate_series(start,stop,step) includes the endpoint if the sequence reaches it. The step must not be zero. A positive step with start greater than stop returns no rows; NULL inputs also return no rows.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: FROM generate_series(1,5) creates five rows. AS s(n) names the table expression and its output column; ORDER BY n specifies display order.
sections.code: SELECT n FROM generate_series(1,5) AS s(n) ORDER BY n;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The numeric example returns 1 through 5, including both endpoints.
sections.code: SELECT n FROM generate_series(1,5) AS s(n) ORDER BY n;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: LATERAL creates a separate daily series for each booking. The last generated date is check_out-1, so checkout day is excluded before the values are cast to dates.
sections.code: SELECT b.id AS booking_id,n.day::date AS night FROM bookings b CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(b.check_in,b.check_out-1,INTERVAL '1 day') n(day) ORDER BY b.id,night;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The small example has five rows under n. These rows are generated; no stored table had to contain those numbers.

n
—
1
2
3
4
5

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Do not include checkout as an occupied night. A calendar LEFT JOIN creates a placeholder for an empty day: count a non-NULL event key rather than count(*). Time-zone-aware series need an explicit calendar/time-zone policy near clock changes.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: LATERAL lets a row-producing expression use the preceding row. A LEFT JOIN to a generated calendar can fill missing reporting periods.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check both endpoints, an empty interval, and a one-night booking. Make sure expansion creates the expected number of rows per booking.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Generate the required domain first, then join or expand the stored data with clear boundaries.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A SQL function gives a reusable calculation or query a name, typed arguments, and a declared result type. It can then be called in SQL expressions.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A shared calculation, such as a tax rule, is easier to reuse when its inputs and result are explicit.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE FUNCTION declares the interface and LANGUAGE sql supplies the body language. Volatility is a promise to the planner: IMMUTABLE depends only on arguments, STABLE stays consistent within a statement, and VOLATILE allows changes or side effects and is the default.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: add_vat accepts numeric and returns numeric. $$ encloses the function body without ordinary quote escaping. round(amount*1.20,2) adds 20 percent and rounds to two decimal places.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION add_vat(amount numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT round(amount*1.20,2) $$;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Creating add_vat defines the calculation; it does not apply it to every product. A later call such as add_vat(price) computes a value.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION add_vat(amount numeric) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT round(amount*1.20,2) $$;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: product_label reads products by its pid argument. STABLE is appropriate for this table lookup; IMMUTABLE would falsely promise that a product name can never change for the same ID.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION product_label(pid integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$ SELECT name FROM products WHERE id=pid $$;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker calls add_vat on product prices after creating the function. For example, 12.50 becomes 15.00. These are check-query results, not direct CREATE FUNCTION output.

id | gross_price
— | —
1 | 15.00
2 | 2.40
3 | 90.00
4 | 300.00
5 | 18.00
6 | 54.00
7 | 9.60
8 | 4.80

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A wrong IMMUTABLE declaration can let the planner reuse a stale value. NULL behavior should be deliberate; RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT skips calls for NULL arguments. Elevated SECURITY DEFINER functions require careful privilege and search_path design.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Views package a relation; functions expose typed arguments and results. PL/pgSQL adds procedural steps when one SQL body is insufficient.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check input and return types, rounding, and NULL behavior. Choose volatility from what the function actually reads or changes, not from the speed you want.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Give reusable logic a clear interface and an honest volatility declaration.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: PL/pgSQL is PostgreSQL's procedural language. It adds variables, decisions, loops, and error handling around SQL statements.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Some rules need intermediate values or branches that are clearer as a short program than as one expression.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DECLARE introduces local variables. BEGIN ... END groups statements; it does not begin or commit a transaction. IF ... THEN, ELSIF, ELSE, and END IF select a branch. RETURN supplies a function's result; := assigns a variable.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: stock_label checks qty in order: zero first, then below 10, otherwise ready. The $$ delimiters enclose the body; semicolons separate its statements.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION stock_label(qty integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$ BEGIN IF qty=0 THEN RETURN 'empty'; ELSIF qty<10 THEN RETURN 'low'; ELSE RETURN 'ready'; END IF; END $$;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: With the fixture's nonnegative stock, 0 gives empty, 1 through 9 give low, and 10 or more give ready. These branches alone do not validate arbitrary input.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION stock_label(qty integer) RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE AS $$ BEGIN IF qty=0 THEN RETURN 'empty'; ELSIF qty<10 THEN RETURN 'low'; ELSE RETURN 'ready'; END IF; END $$;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: booking_charge declares charge, stores a query result with SELECT ... INTO charge, then returns it. Date subtraction gives nights before multiplication by the nightly rate.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION booking_charge(bid integer) RETURNS numeric LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$ DECLARE charge numeric; BEGIN SELECT (check_out-check_in)*nightly_rate INTO charge FROM bookings WHERE id=bid; RETURN charge; END $$;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker calls stock_label for each product. Retail shows low for stock 5 and 8, empty for 0, and ready for the other displayed stocks.

id | label
— | —
1 | ready
2 | ready
3 | ready
4 | low
5 | empty
6 | low
7 | ready
8 | ready

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: In this function NULL qty reaches ELSE because neither IF condition is true; a negative qty gives low. Handle such input explicitly when required. SELECT INTO without STRICT gives NULLs when no row is found and keeps only the first row when several match. Prefer a set-based query to an unnecessary loop.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A SQL function can be simpler for one calculation. PL/pgSQL BEGIN/END are block syntax, unlike SQL BEGIN/COMMIT transaction commands.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace each branch, including NULL and boundary 10. For a lookup, check the missing-row case and whether the query can return several rows.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use procedural steps when they clarify the rule, and keep blocks distinct from transactions.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A procedure is a named server-side operation invoked with CALL. Unlike a function, it is not called as a value inside SELECT.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: It can give a multi-step business operation one clear interface, such as restocking a product.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE PROCEDURE declares parameters, a language, and a body; CALL runs it. A procedure may have output parameters, but it has no function-style RETURNS clause. In PL/pgSQL, BEGIN/END groups the body rather than starting a transaction.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: restock takes a product ID and unit count. The UPDATE adds units to stock only where id=pid. CALL restock(1,7) supplies the arguments.
sections.code: CREATE PROCEDURE restock(pid integer,units integer) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE products SET stock=stock+units WHERE id=pid; END $$; CALL restock(1,7);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: On Retail, product 1's stock changes from 40 to 47. Other products stay unchanged.
sections.code: CREATE PROCEDURE restock(pid integer,units integer) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE products SET stock=stock+units WHERE id=pid; END $$; CALL restock(1,7);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: mark_inventory_checked accepts a date and updates every inventory row. The absence of WHERE is intentional because all records need the new checked date.
sections.code: CREATE PROCEDURE mark_inventory_checked(as_of date) LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE inventory SET updated_on=as_of; END $$; CALL mark_inventory_checked(DATE '2024-08-15');

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker reads products after CALL and shows stock 47 for ID 1. The procedure call does not itself return these product rows.

id | stock
— | —
1 | 47
2 | 120
3 | 12
4 | 5
5 | 0
6 | 8
7 | 50
8 | 20

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A missing pid makes this UPDATE affect no rows; negative units reduce stock. Add explicit validation when the business rule requires it. Transaction control inside procedures is limited to eligible top-level CALL/DO chains and is not allowed inside an explicit transaction block; these examples leave transaction boundaries to the caller.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Functions return values in queries. Procedures describe operations; both still obey constraints and permissions.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the intended row scope and argument meaning. Compare a targeted update with the deliberate all-row inventory update.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define an operation with CREATE PROCEDURE and run it with CALL; do not assume it validates every input automatically.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A trigger runs a function automatically when a specified table event occurs. A row trigger runs once for each affected row.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A shared write rule can apply even when different applications insert or update the table.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CREATE TRIGGER declares timing, event, table, and row or statement scope. For INSERT, NEW contains the proposed row; UPDATE provides NEW and OLD; DELETE provides OLD. A BEFORE row trigger can change NEW before storage.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: trim_customer_name returns trigger. It assigns trim(NEW.name), then RETURN NEW lets the insertion continue with the edited row. BEFORE INSERT and FOR EACH ROW attach it to every inserted customer.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION trim_customer_name() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.name:=trim(NEW.name); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER normalize_name BEFORE INSERT ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION trim_customer_name(); INSERT INTO customers(id,name,joined_on) VALUES(60,'  Zara  ',DATE '2024-08-01');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The inserted name has surrounding spaces. The stored customer 60 is named Zara after the trigger removes them.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION trim_customer_name() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.name:=trim(NEW.name); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER normalize_name BEFORE INSERT ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION trim_customer_name(); INSERT INTO customers(id,name,joined_on) VALUES(60,'  Zara  ',DATE '2024-08-01');

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The product trigger rounds the proposed price to one decimal place before insertion. The stored numeric(10,2) value may still display two decimal digits.
sections.code: CREATE FUNCTION round_product_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN NEW.price:=round(NEW.price,1); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER product_round BEFORE INSERT ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION round_product_price(); INSERT INTO products(id,name,category,price,stock) VALUES(60,'Clip','Office',1.26,5);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker reads the customers table after insertion. Zara appears without surrounding spaces; the pre-existing customer rows are unchanged.

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada
2 | Ben
3 | Cleo
4 | Davi
5 | Eli
6 | Fara
60 | Zara

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Returning NULL from a BEFORE row trigger skips that row's operation; RETURN NEW is important for INSERT/UPDATE. A row trigger and a statement trigger are different scopes. Avoid accidental recursion and use a constraint when it expresses a simple validity rule more directly.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: A DEFAULT provides a value; a BEFORE trigger can transform a supplied value. An AFTER trigger is suited to follow-up recording after a successful row operation.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the stored value, not just the submitted INSERT text. Confirm the trigger's timing, event, scope, and return value.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use BEFORE row triggers for deliberate row transformation, and return the row that should be stored.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An audit trigger records what changed in a separate history table. For an update, it can keep the old and new values side by side.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A change history helps explain price adjustments or record newly added customers.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OLD contains the previous row and NEW the new row for UPDATE. An AFTER row trigger records the completed row change. Its return value is ignored, so RETURN NULL does not cancel the update.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: price_audit holds product_id, old_price, and new_price. AFTER UPDATE OF price fires when price is targeted by SET. The function inserts OLD.price and NEW.price into the history table.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE price_audit(product_id integer,old_price numeric,new_price numeric); CREATE FUNCTION audit_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO price_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); RETURN NULL; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER price_history AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_price(); UPDATE products SET price=price+2 WHERE id=1;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: Adding 2 to product 1's price records an audit row from 12.50 to 14.50.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE price_audit(product_id integer,old_price numeric,new_price numeric); CREATE FUNCTION audit_price() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO price_audit VALUES(NEW.id,OLD.price,NEW.price); RETURN NULL; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER price_history AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_price(); UPDATE products SET price=price+2 WHERE id=1;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The customer example uses AFTER INSERT to copy the inserted ID and name. INSERT has NEW but no old customer row to record.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE customer_audit(customer_id integer,name text); CREATE FUNCTION audit_customer_insert() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO customer_audit VALUES(NEW.id,NEW.name); RETURN NULL; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER customer_insertion AFTER INSERT ON customers FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_customer_insert(); INSERT INTO customers(id,name,joined_on) VALUES(61,'Yara',DATE '2024-08-01');

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker reads price_audit and shows one change for product 1. The audit insert and original update belong to the same transaction.

product_id | old_price | new_price
— | — | —
1 | 12.50 | 14.50

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: UPDATE OF price can fire even for SET price=price. To record only actual changes in another design, compare OLD.price IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.price. Rollback also removes transactional audit rows, so this is not a permanent log of failed attempts. Production history needs access rules and retention.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: BEFORE can alter the row being written; AFTER can record the result. IS DISTINCT FROM compares changes safely when values may be NULL.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the old/new pair and the audit row count. Distinguish a column mentioned in UPDATE from a value that really changed.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Audit deliberate events with OLD and NEW, and remember that this history shares the transaction's outcome.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Full-text search finds words and related word forms in documents. PostgreSQL first reduces words to searchable forms called lexemes.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Use it for articles or help pages when matching different forms of a word is more useful than finding an exact substring.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: to_tsvector prepares the document; a tsquery describes the search. The @@ operator asks whether they match. Use the same language configuration on both sides.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: 'english' selects English word rules. body supplies the document. plainto_tsquery treats SQL as ordinary search text; WHERE keeps matches and ORDER BY id sorts them.
sections.code: SELECT id,title FROM documents WHERE to_tsvector('english',body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english','SQL') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small query searches document bodies for SQL and returns only their IDs and titles. It does not search the title column.
sections.code: SELECT id,title FROM documents WHERE to_tsvector('english',body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english','SQL') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: phraseto_tsquery searches for SQL queries in that order, accounting for word positions. This is narrower than requiring both words anywhere in a document.
sections.code: SELECT id,title FROM documents WHERE to_tsvector('english',body) @@ phraseto_tsquery('english','SQL queries') ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
On Retail, SQL guide is the only matching document. The result shows its id and title, not the transformed search representation.

id | title
— | —
1 | SQL guide

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: ILIKE matches character patterns; full-text search uses language rules and can remove common words. A search configuration must suit the document language.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare LIKE and regular expressions with word-based search. For larger collections, GIN can index prepared tsvector values; ranking is a separate calculation.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Test a single word, several words, and a phrase. Check which column is searched before deciding that a missing match is an error.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Prepare the document and search with matching language rules, then use @@ to test each document.

A text-search configuration affects stemming and stop words. ILIKE and full-text search answer different questions.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: An index is an extra structure that helps PostgreSQL find rows. A B-tree supports equality, ranges, and ordered access; a Hash index supports equality.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Indexes can reduce the rows a query must inspect. They also consume storage and add work to inserts, updates, and deletes.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The planner compares possible ways to read a table. Selectivity means how small a fraction of rows a condition matches; fewer matches often make an index more useful.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: CREATE INDEX names the index. ON orders selects its table; USING btree selects the method; (customer_id,ordered_on) gives the key columns in order.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_date ON orders USING btree(customer_id,ordered_on);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example builds an index for customer order histories. It creates a structure; it does not return the indexed rows or guarantee its use.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_date ON orders USING btree(customer_id,ordered_on);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The reporting query counts products below 20 and all products together. Comparing these counts shows how much of the table that condition selects.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) FILTER(WHERE price<20) AS matching_rows,count(*) AS total_rows FROM products;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker confirms the btree method and the two key columns. This inspection table is separate from CREATE INDEX's command response.

amname | key1 | key2
— | — | —
btree | customer_id | ordered_on

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A sequential scan can be sensible on a small table. A multicolumn B-tree is usually most effective when conditions constrain its leading columns, though other access strategies exist.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Connect indexes with WHERE, ORDER BY, and EXPLAIN. An ordinary index speeds access; a unique index also enforces a uniqueness rule.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the method and column order, then reason about the matching fraction. Do not use tiny-fixture timings as evidence of a production speedup.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose an index for actual lookup conditions and ordering needs, then confirm the planner's choice with a plan.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Index methods solve different search problems. GIN finds components inside collections; GiST supports searches such as range overlap; BRIN summarizes neighboring table pages.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A JSON containment query and a date-range overlap query need different kinds of information. One index method cannot efficiently serve every operator.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: An operator class tells an index how a data type's operations work. Choose a supported method and operator class for the condition you plan to use.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: USING gin(attributes) builds a GIN index on the JSONB attributes column. The default JSONB operator class supports several searches, including containment.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX products_attributes_gin ON products USING gin(attributes);

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small example indexes product attributes. It prepares an access path for suitable JSONB conditions without changing any product values.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX products_attributes_gin ON products USING gin(attributes);

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The BRIN example summarizes occurred_at across page ranges. It is especially useful on large tables when nearby rows tend to have nearby timestamps.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX events_time_brin ON events USING brin(occurred_at);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker identifies a gin index on attributes. It verifies the structure, not that every query will become faster.

amname | key1
— | —
gin | attributes

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A matching method is only a starting point. BRIN may still inspect many rows; GIN can be costly to update; supported operators vary by operator class.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Use GiST with range overlap, GIN with arrays or JSONB, and EXPLAIN to see whether a specific query can use the index.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Match each index to its intended operator. Consider table size, value order, and update frequency before comparing access methods.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose the search operation first, then an index method and operator class that support it.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A partial index stores only qualifying rows. An expression index stores a calculated search key. INCLUDE stores extra columns alongside the key.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: These options tailor indexes to frequent queries, such as pending orders, case-normalized email searches, or reports needing a few extra values.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The planner must recognize that a query satisfies a partial index's condition. Expression indexes need matching expressions and immutable calculations; included columns are payload, not search keys.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: ON orders(ordered_on) indexes order dates. WHERE status='pending' restricts the index to pending orders; this WHERE belongs to the index definition.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_pending_date ON orders(ordered_on) WHERE status='pending';

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small example omits paid and cancelled orders from the index. A query for pending orders may then use a smaller structure.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_pending_date ON orders(ordered_on) WHERE status='pending';

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The covering index searches by customer_id and also stores total and ordered_on. These included columns can avoid table reads when visibility information allows it.
sections.code: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_cover ON orders(customer_id) INCLUDE(total,ordered_on);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker shows ordered_on as the key and the pending-status condition. The table describes the index definition, not order data.

key1 | predicate
— | —
ordered_on | (status = 'pending'::text)

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: INCLUDE does not guarantee an index-only scan. The planner may not prove a partial condition from a parameter, and a different expression may not match an expression index.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare a search key with an included value. Relate index-only scans to VACUUM's visibility information and partial indexes to Boolean conditions.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Read each query and index side by side. Check the filter, expression, key order, and which selected columns are actually covered.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Specialized indexes help only when their definitions match the workload; every extra column also has a storage and write cost.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A query plan describes how PostgreSQL intends to produce a result. Its nodes are operations such as scanning, sorting, joining, and grouping.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: EXPLAIN helps you see where work is planned before guessing which index or rewrite might help.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Child nodes feed rows to their parents. Costs and row counts are estimates; cost is a planning unit, not elapsed milliseconds. Plain EXPLAIN normally does not execute the statement.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) describes the following SELECT and hides estimated cost details. The products filter still means price greater than 50.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE price>50;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The filtered-scan example asks how PostgreSQL will find expensive products. The returned rows describe a plan rather than products themselves.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE price>50;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The grouped-revenue example adds aggregation by status. Find the scan that supplies orders and the node that combines rows into status totals.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT status,sum(total) FROM orders GROUP BY status;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The sample plan uses Seq Scan and a price filter. That means reading products and checking the condition; the tiny table can make this a sensible choice.

QUERY PLAN
—
Seq Scan on products
  Filter: (price > '50'::numeric)

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Do not treat every sequential scan as a problem. Plan shape may change with data, statistics, settings, or PostgreSQL versions.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Connect scans to indexes, row estimates to ANALYZE statistics, and plan trees to the logical operations in SELECT.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: For each plan, identify the data source, filter, and any sort or aggregate. Explain what each node contributes to the final result.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Read a plan as a flow of rows, and distinguish an estimated plan from measured execution.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs a statement and reports what its plan actually did, including returned rows and execution counts.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Actual measurements help you discover where estimated row counts were wrong or unexpectedly much work occurred.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Compare estimates with actual rows when both are displayed. For repeated nodes, actual rows are averages per execution; loops shows how many executions occurred.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: ANALYZE executes the SELECT. TIMING OFF hides per-node timing, SUMMARY OFF hides the overall summary, and COSTS OFF hides estimates. PostgreSQL 18 enables buffer reporting with ANALYZE by default.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF) SELECT id FROM products WHERE stock=0;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The stock example reads products and retains those with stock=0. The plan reports retained rows and rows rejected by the filter.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF) SELECT id FROM products WHERE stock=0;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The order-item example counts every input row into one result. Distinguish the scan's input count from the aggregate's single output row.
sections.code: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF, COSTS OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM order_items;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
On Retail, one product has zero stock and seven are rejected. Buffer lines describe page access; their exact counts can vary between runs.

QUERY PLAN
—
Seq Scan on products (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
  Filter: (stock = 0)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 7
  Buffers: shared hit=1
Planning:
  Buffers: shared hit=80

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: ANALYZE on UPDATE or DELETE really changes data. A rollback can undo ordinary database changes, but not every possible external or sequence side effect.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Unlike the standalone ANALYZE maintenance command, EXPLAIN ANALYZE measures execution. BUFFERS describes page activity rather than just elapsed time.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Read rows and loops together. Compare where rows enter, are removed, and leave each operation without relying on identical timing or buffer counts.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Use measured plans to explain work, remembering that collecting measurements executes the statement.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A useful optimization changes how a query does its work while preserving what the result means: its rows, duplicates, NULLs, and required order.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A report is only useful when it remains correct. Improve unnecessary work after defining who and what must appear.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: First identify what one output row represents. Then check join conditions, filters, and grouping before comparing alternative plans on representative data.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: LEFT JOIN keeps every customer. The paid filter belongs in ON; count(o.id) counts matching orders, GROUP BY c.id summarizes each customer, and ORDER BY fixes the result order.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id,count(o.id) AS paid_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The repaired report keeps customers with no paid orders and gives them a zero count. WHERE o.status='paid' would remove those customers.
sections.code: SELECT c.id AS customer_id,count(o.id) AS paid_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY c.id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The June example uses a lower date bound and an exclusive July bound. This captures one month's dates without applying a function to each stored date.
sections.code: SELECT id,ordered_on FROM orders WHERE ordered_on>=DATE '2024-06-01' AND ordered_on<DATE '2024-07-01' ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Fara remains in the sample with paid_count=0. Her presence is a correctness check, not an optional display detail.

customer_id | paid_count
— | —
1 | 3
2 | 2
3 | 1
4 | 1
5 | 1
6 | 0

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Moving filters across an outer join can change its meaning. An index-friendly condition does not guarantee a faster plan on every dataset.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Relate this work to LEFT JOIN, EXISTS, NULL handling, and date ranges. Equivalent results must be established before comparing execution costs.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check missing customers, repeated matches, boundary dates, and NULLs. Only then investigate whether a rewrite reduces work.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Preserve the report's rules first; use plans and realistic data to justify performance changes.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: PostgreSQL uses statistics to estimate how many rows a condition will match. ANALYZE refreshes these summaries from table data.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Good estimates help the planner choose scans and joins. A common value and a rare value may justify different plans.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Statistics describe distributions, such as frequent values and distinct-value estimates. Extended statistics can describe relationships among columns; CREATE STATISTICS defines them and ANALYZE collects them.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: ANALYZE products refreshes statistics. The following SELECT groups by category and count(*) reports actual product counts; these are two separate commands.
sections.code: ANALYZE products; SELECT category,count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example both refreshes statistics and shows the category distribution. Its displayed counts come from SELECT, not ANALYZE's internal sample.
sections.code: ANALYZE products; SELECT category,count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY category;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The status report divides each status count by the total number of orders. Casting to numeric preserves a fractional share before rounding.
sections.code: SELECT status,count(*) AS order_count,round(count(*)::numeric/(SELECT count(*) FROM orders),4) AS share FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
Retail has two Home products, three Office products, and three Tech products. The shown table is an exact grouped count for this fixture.

category | product_count
— | —
Home | 2
Office | 3
Tech | 3

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Statistics can become stale after major changes and estimates need not be exact. Raising the statistics target adds analysis work and does not repair incorrect SQL.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare estimated rows in EXPLAIN with real counts. ANALYZE updates planner information; VACUUM handles old row versions and can optionally run ANALYZE too.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Inspect distributions and consider whether columns are related. Verify extended-statistics definitions separately from whether a particular plan uses them.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Refresh statistics after meaningful data changes, and treat planner row counts as estimates rather than guarantees.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: PostgreSQL can keep older row versions while other transactions still need them. VACUUM removes versions that are no longer needed and makes space reusable.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Frequent updates and deletes leave cleanup work behind. Maintenance also prevents transaction-ID wraparound and supports efficient visibility checks.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Ordinary VACUUM usually allows reads and writes. Autovacuum performs routine maintenance. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table, needs extra space, and takes a much stronger lock.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: VACUUM (ANALYZE) products cleans the table and refreshes its statistics. Run it outside an explicit transaction block.
sections.code: VACUUM (ANALYZE) products;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small example maintains products. Its checker inspects the row estimate and whether pages are marked all-visible; VACUUM itself does not return this table.
sections.code: VACUUM (ANALYZE) products;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The catalog query reports each current-schema table's persistence code. Ordinary, unlogged, and temporary tables have different durability and lifetime rules.
sections.code: SELECT c.relname AS table_name,c.relpersistence::text AS persistence FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname=current_schema() AND c.relkind='r' ORDER BY c.relname;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker reports eight estimated product rows and visible pages on Retail. The t value means true; this is maintenance-state inspection, not a data query from VACUUM.

estimated_rows | has_visible_pages
— | —
8 | t

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Ordinary VACUUM usually reuses space rather than fully shrinking the file. Long-running transactions can delay cleanup; VACUUM cannot run inside BEGIN…COMMIT.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Connect cleanup to MVCC and index-only scans. ANALYZE describes data for planning; it does not replace removal of obsolete row versions.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Keep maintenance commands standalone. Distinguish row estimates, visibility information, and table persistence from the business values stored in rows.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Maintain changing tables regularly; use ordinary VACUUM, statistics, and monitoring together rather than assuming deletion immediately frees disk space.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Performance troubleshooting means finding evidence for why a query is slow, rather than changing SQL at random.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: The same query can behave differently with larger data, uneven value frequencies, cached pages, or competing work.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Record the query and its parameters, confirm the result rules, inspect its plan, and compare estimated with actual rows. Change one likely cause, then measure again.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: WHERE removes unknown customer IDs. GROUP BY customer_id counts each customer's orders; descending count and then customer_id make the busiest customers easy to inspect.
sections.code: SELECT customer_id,count(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY order_count DESC,customer_id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The order-count example reveals uneven activity between customers. Such uneven distributions can explain why one parameter value is more expensive than another.
sections.code: SELECT customer_id,count(*) AS order_count FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY order_count DESC,customer_id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The repeated-price query groups products by price and keeps groups with more than one row. On another dataset it can reveal duplicates absent from the basic fixture.
sections.code: SELECT price,count(*) AS product_count FROM products GROUP BY price HAVING count(*)>1 ORDER BY price;

sections.body: One quick run does not establish a speedup. Include planning overhead, page-cache effects, current load, and representative parameter values in comparisons.

sections.title: Connections

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A transaction groups changes into one unit. ACID means all-or-nothing changes, preservation of defined rules, controlled interaction with other transactions, and durable committed data under normal durability settings.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A transfer should not debit one account while leaving the credit undone. Readers also need a predictable view when other transactions change data.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MVCC keeps row versions for a snapshot, a view of visible data. READ COMMITTED uses a fresh snapshot per statement; REPEATABLE READ keeps a transaction snapshot from its first non-control statement.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: current_setting('transaction_isolation') returns the active isolation level. AS isolation_level gives that value a readable result-column name.
sections.code: SELECT current_setting('transaction_isolation') AS isolation_level;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small query inspects isolation without changing it. This practice environment normally uses read committed.
sections.code: SELECT current_setting('transaction_isolation') AS isolation_level;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The SERIALIZABLE example starts a transaction, subtracts 5 from account 2, then rolls back. The balance change is discarded.
sections.code: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-5 WHERE id=2; ROLLBACK;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The sample reports read committed. This one-session query cannot show what a second session would see during a competing transaction.

isolation_level
—
read committed

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: SERIALIZABLE can abort a transaction to prevent inconsistent concurrent outcomes; retry the whole transaction. PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED, and constraints remain necessary at every level.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Relate snapshots to old row versions and VACUUM. Isolation controls concurrent visibility; atomicity controls whether a transaction's changes succeed together.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Predict balances after COMMIT and ROLLBACK. Use the written concurrency scenario to compare snapshots; actual competing sessions are outside this workspace.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Choose transaction boundaries and isolation deliberately, preserve data rules, and handle failures with a whole-transaction recovery policy.

exercises.title: Explain two reads and one concurrent commit
exercises.prompt: A transaction reads an account balance. Another transaction commits a new balance. The first transaction reads the balance again. Explain the possible result under READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ, and explain why a SERIALIZABLE application still needs retry logic. This written answer is self-assessed against a model explanation.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT true AS discussed;
hints: Separate a statement snapshot from a transaction snapshot.
Consider whether the second SELECT obtains a new snapshot.
Distinguish isolation guarantees from a promise that every transaction will commit.
exercises.explanation: Read your answer against the model, identify missing points, and mark it reviewed when you can explain the distinction in your own words.
exercises.modelAnswer: Under READ COMMITTED, each statement obtains a new snapshot. The second SELECT can see the newly committed balance. Under REPEATABLE READ, both reads use the transaction snapshot, so a newly committed external change is not visible to the second read. SERIALIZABLE adds protection against serialization anomalies, but PostgreSQL can abort a transaction with a serialization failure. The application must retry the entire transaction, with bounded retry policy and no duplicated external side effects.

ROLLBACK TO is not a full ROLLBACK.
Commit the surviving transaction state.
exercises.explanation: A savepoint rolls back only work after its creation. The earlier account change remains eligible for commit.

lessons.title: Row locks, NOWAIT, and SKIP LOCKED

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A row lock coordinates transactions that want to change the same row. SELECT … FOR UPDATE reads rows and locks them against conflicting changes.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Locking is useful when a decision and the following update must be based on protected rows, such as checking accounts before a transfer.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Ordinary readers can usually still read locked rows. Conflicting writers wait; NOWAIT reports an error immediately, while SKIP LOCKED leaves unavailable rows out of the result.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: WHERE chooses accounts 1 and 2; ORDER BY id sets the requested order; FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows until transaction end.
sections.code: SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN(1,2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The account example returns balances while taking locks. In a real application, keep dependent reads and updates in the same explicit transaction.
sections.code: SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN(1,2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The queue example takes the oldest pending order by date and id. LIMIT 1 bounds the claim; SKIP LOCKED lets another worker choose a different available row.
sections.code: SELECT id,total FROM orders WHERE status='pending' ORDER BY ordered_on,id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The sample shows accounts 1 and 2 with their original balances. With no competing session, there is no waiting or skipping to observe.

id | balance
— | —
1 | 1000.00
2 | 500.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: SKIP LOCKED omits rows, so it is unsuitable for a complete financial report. NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED affect row locks; required table locks can still wait. An autocommitted statement releases locks when its transaction ends.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare row locks with MVCC snapshots and table locks. FOR KEY SHARE is a weaker row-lock mode useful for protecting referenced keys.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check the selected rows and lock clause. Explain the difference between waiting, failing immediately, and skipping; this single-operation workspace cannot demonstrate competing workers.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Lock only the rows needed, keep transactions short, and choose waiting behavior that matches the application.

exercises.title: Lock a stable account set
exercises.prompt: Return id and balance for accounts 1 and 2 ordered by id using FOR UPDATE.
exercises.solutionSQL: SELECT id,balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN(1,2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A deadlock is a cycle of transactions waiting for one another's locks. A connection pool reuses database connections instead of opening a new one for every request.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Consistent lock order reduces deadlock risk. A pool limits connection overhead and load, but does not remove transaction failures or data-consistency requirements.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PostgreSQL detects deadlocks and aborts one transaction. After deadlock or serialization failure, retry the whole transaction with bounded delays; make externally visible actions safe to repeat.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: BEGIN groups the transfer. Separate FOR UPDATE reads lock account 1 before 3; two UPDATE commands move 15; COMMIT keeps both changes.
sections.code: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=3 FOR UPDATE; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-15 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+15 WHERE id=3; COMMIT;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The ordered-lock example applies a consistent account order. It does not create an actual deadlock because the workspace has no competing learner session.
sections.code: BEGIN; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id=3 FOR UPDATE; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-15 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+15 WHERE id=3; COMMIT;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The second transfer moves 20 from account 1 to 2 together. The total across accounts must remain unchanged.
sections.code: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-20 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance+20 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker shows balances 985, 500, and 765 after the first transfer. It inspects committed state rather than the intermediate SELECT output.

id | balance
— | —
1 | 985.00
2 | 500.00
3 | 765.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Retrying only the last failed command is unsafe. Transaction pooling may use another server connection next time, so do not rely on persistent session settings or temporary tables.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Use transaction-local settings for transaction-scoped behavior. An idempotency key prevents a retried request from applying the same business operation twice.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace lock order and account totals. For retry exercises, check that a repeated request cannot debit again and that local settings end with the transaction.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Short transactions, consistent lock order, bounded retries, and repeat-safe writes solve different parts of reliable concurrent work.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A role is a PostgreSQL identity. It can own objects and receive permissions; LOGIN allows it to open a database session.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Least privilege means granting only what each job needs. A reporting account, for example, usually needs to read selected tables rather than administer the server.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GRANT adds privileges and REVOKE removes grants. Ownership carries object-management rights. PUBLIC means all roles, including roles created later.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: has_table_privilege checks a named permission. current_user identifies the active role, 'products' identifies the table, and 'SELECT' is the privilege being tested.
sections.code: SELECT has_table_privilege(current_user,'products','SELECT') AS can_select;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small query asks whether the current learner can read products. It inspects permission without adding any rights.
sections.code: SELECT has_table_privilege(current_user,'products','SELECT') AS can_select;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: REVOKE ALL ON products FROM PUBLIC removes public grants on that table. It does not transfer ownership or remove rights inherited through another role.
sections.code: REVOKE ALL ON products FROM PUBLIC;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The sample returns t, meaning the current role can SELECT from products. It does not mean the role can administer PostgreSQL.

can_select
—
t

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Removing one grant may leave access through another role or ownership. Schema USAGE and table permissions are separate. These permissions do not give access to files on the server.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare permission to ownership and RLS. The learner role is intentionally unable to create privileged roles, administer the server, or install unrestricted extensions.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Inspect specific privileges and administrative flags. Explain which permission source is changed by REVOKE before assuming access has disappeared.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Grant the minimum required rights, account for ownership and inherited access, and verify permissions from the intended role.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: SQL injection occurs when application input becomes part of SQL syntax. Value parameters keep input separate from the command's structure.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A customer name may contain quotes or SQL-looking text. It must remain a name, not become a condition that changes which rows are returned.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The application sends a fixed query with placeholders and binds values through its database driver's API. Parameters represent values; table names and keywords need separate validated composition.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: PREPARE lookup_customer(text) declares one text parameter. In WHERE name=$1, $1 refers to that value. EXECUTE supplies Ada for this prepared statement.
sections.code: PREPARE lookup_customer(text) AS SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name=$1 ORDER BY id; EXECUTE lookup_customer('Ada');

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The lookup example returns Ada's record through an exact name comparison. Its SQL structure stays the same when the parameter value changes.
sections.code: PREPARE lookup_customer(text) AS SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name=$1 ORDER BY id; EXECUTE lookup_customer('Ada');

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The hostile-looking name Ada' OR true -- is supplied as one text value. Because nobody has that literal name, the intended result is empty.
sections.code: PREPARE exact_name(text) AS SELECT id,name FROM customers WHERE name=$1 ORDER BY id; EXECUTE exact_name('Ada'' OR true --');

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The small example returns id 1 and name Ada. Those rows come from the bound name comparison, not from interpreting input as SQL.

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Do not concatenate user input or rely on blocking words such as DROP. In the handwritten EXECUTE example, doubled quotes express a literal; application code should use driver binding instead.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Prepared statements also support reuse, but safe value binding does not require manually writing SQL PREPARE. Authorization and allowed identifier choices remain separate responsibilities.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check that changed values cannot change the query structure. Distinguish value placeholders from dynamic identifiers and keep output columns and ordering unchanged.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Keep SQL structure fixed, bind external values with the driver, and validate any separately composed identifiers.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Row-level security, or RLS, controls which table rows a role may read or change. It adds row rules to ordinary object permissions.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A shared table may hold data for different users or teams. RLS can enforce row access centrally instead of depending on every application query to remember a filter.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ENABLE activates RLS. USING tests existing rows; WITH CHECK tests proposed new values. With RLS enabled and no applicable policy, access is denied by default for roles subject to RLS.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: FORCE makes the table owner obey RLS too. CREATE POLICY … FOR SELECT USING(vip) allows reading VIP rows; the final SELECT shows the permitted customers.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE customers ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE customers FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY vip_only ON customers FOR SELECT USING(vip); SELECT id,name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The example forces the owner-held customers table through its SELECT policy. Customers whose vip value is false are hidden.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE customers ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE customers FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY vip_only ON customers FOR SELECT USING(vip); SELECT id,name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The accounts policy permits balances of at least 500. This is a SELECT rule, not a constraint preventing smaller balances from existing.
sections.code: ALTER TABLE accounts ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE accounts FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY funded_accounts ON accounts FOR SELECT USING(balance>=500);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker sees Ada and Davi in Retail after the VIP policy. It inspects policy-filtered rows, not just whether policy metadata exists.

id | name
— | —
1 | Ada
4 | Davi

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Owners normally bypass RLS; superusers and BYPASSRLS roles still bypass it despite FORCE. Table privileges are still required. RLS does not govern whole-table operations such as TRUNCATE.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Permissive policies combine with OR; restrictive policies add AND requirements. Review views and SECURITY DEFINER functions carefully because execution identity affects access.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Check both permitted and hidden rows. When combining policies, work through the Boolean conditions and distinguish row visibility from allowed inserted or updated values.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: RLS adds per-row authorization; test it as the intended role and account for ownership, bypass rights, and policy combinations.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A useful backup contains enough information to restore the required data and structure. A copied result table is only a small part of that job.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: Backups protect against mistakes, loss, and corruption. A recovery plan must say how much data loss is acceptable and how quickly service must return.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: pg_dump creates a consistent logical export of one database. Plain SQL is restored with tools such as psql; archive formats use pg_restore. Roles and other cluster-wide objects need a separate plan.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: CREATE TABLE account_snapshot AS runs the SELECT and creates a table from its output. This copies columns and rows, not the original keys, indexes, or full database configuration.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE account_snapshot AS SELECT id,owner,balance FROM accounts;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The snapshot example copies account IDs, owners, and balances inside the practice database. It neither creates an external backup file nor runs a host command.
sections.code: CREATE TABLE account_snapshot AS SELECT id,owner,balance FROM accounts;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The orphan-check query looks for non-NULL customer IDs without a customer. After a restore, checks like this complement row counts, totals, and application tests.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) AS orphan_count FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.id=o.customer_id);

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The checker reads the three copied accounts. Matching these rows proves this copy's contents, not that a complete backup and restore process works.

id | owner | balance
— | — | —
1 | Ada | 1000.00
2 | Ben | 500.00
3 | Cleo | 750.00

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A successful dump command is not a tested recovery. Plan retention, access protection, globals, and restore testing; point-in-time recovery additionally needs an appropriate physical backup and WAL archive.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare logical export, row copying, and physical recovery. The SQL workspace teaches safe checks; it does not execute pg_dump or provision an operational backup service.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Verify copied data and reconciliation totals. Explain what each check misses, especially constraints, privileges, and objects outside the copied table.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define the recovery goal, preserve everything needed for it, and prove recovery by restoring and checking a separate environment.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Write-ahead logging, WAL, records changes before their data pages are written durably. Replication sends database changes to another server.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: WAL supports crash recovery. Replication can support availability or additional readers, but introduces questions about freshness, failure, and which server may accept writes.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Physical replication replays storage-level WAL. Logical replication transfers selected data changes through publications and subscriptions. Asynchronous replicas can lag; stronger acknowledgement requirements trade latency and availability for durability guarantees.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: pg_is_in_recovery() reports whether the server is in recovery. AS in_recovery names the Boolean result; false normally identifies a writable primary in this example.
sections.code: SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS in_recovery;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small query inspects the bundled server. SQLLY runs one local primary; it does not create a standby or simulate failover.
sections.code: SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS in_recovery;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The status summary compares order counts and amounts by status. It could help compare datasets at a consistent point, but equal totals alone cannot prove identical replicas.
sections.code: SELECT status,count(*) AS row_count,sum(total) AS total_amount FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The sample returns f, meaning false: this server is not in recovery. That result alone does not say whether replication is configured.

in_recovery
—
f

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: A replica is not a historical backup: accidental deletions can propagate. Logical replication has identity and schema-management requirements; failover needs a deliberate plan to avoid conflicting primaries.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Relate WAL to crash recovery and physical backups. Logical replica identity tells PostgreSQL how to identify updated or deleted rows, often through a primary key.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Inspect recovery state and replica-identity metadata. Treat reconciliation queries as checks on data, not as evidence that this workspace provisions replication.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Separate crash recovery, replication, and backup goals; define acceptable lag and failure behavior before choosing an operational setup.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: Operational troubleshooting traces a symptom to a specific cause using database errors, application behavior, and system observations.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: A failed request might reflect bad data, a missing permission, a blocked transaction, or an unavailable server. Those problems require different responses.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Start with the exact error and SQLSTATE, the five-character error code. Confirm connectivity, inspect relevant data and constraints, then investigate activity or locks with appropriate permissions.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: The query counts orders where total<0. AS invalid_total_count labels a direct check of one business rule; it does not check every possible order problem.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) AS invalid_total_count FROM orders WHERE total<0;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The small example verifies that no stored order has a negative total. A zero result means this one condition found no violations.
sections.code: SELECT count(*) AS invalid_total_count FROM orders WHERE total<0;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The constraint report groups available current-schema constraints by table and type. Its results reflect what the current role can see.
sections.code: SELECT table_name,constraint_type,count(*) AS constraint_count FROM information_schema.table_constraints WHERE table_schema=current_schema() GROUP BY table_name,constraint_type ORDER BY table_name,constraint_type;

sections.title: Expected results

sections.title: The idea
sections.body: A recursive query follows a rule repeatedly. It starts with initial rows, then uses each round's rows to find the next round.

sections.title: Why it exists
sections.body: It can walk an organization chart or connected records when the number of levels is unknown in advance.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: WITH RECURSIVE defines an initial term and a recursive term. PostgreSQL repeats the recursive term using a working set and stops when that set produces no rows.

sections.title: Read the syntax
sections.body: numbers(n) names the result and its column. SELECT 1 starts it; UNION ALL appends n+1 while n<5; the final SELECT orders the completed result.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM numbers WHERE n<5) SELECT n FROM numbers ORDER BY n;

sections.title: A small example
sections.body: The number example starts at 1 and reaches 5. The stop condition is tested before adding the next number.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM numbers WHERE n<5) SELECT n FROM numbers ORDER BY n;

sections.title: A realistic use
sections.body: The employee query starts with direct reports of employee 2, then finds their reports. Employee 2 is excluded because the initial rows are their children.
sections.code: WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (SELECT id,name FROM employees WHERE manager_id=2 UNION ALL SELECT e.id,e.name FROM employees e JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id=r.id) SELECT id,name FROM reports ORDER BY id;

sections.title: Expected results
sections.body:
The small result contains 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. ORDER BY n guarantees this display order; recursive processing alone does not define final row order.

n
—
1
2
3
4
5

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: UNION ALL preserves duplicates and does not detect cycles. A link returning to a previous node can run indefinitely unless you prevent revisits or impose an appropriate stopping rule.

sections.title: Connections
sections.body: Compare recursion with ordinary CTEs and self joins. A fixed self join follows a fixed number of levels; recursion follows as many as its rule allows.

sections.title: Practice deliberately
sections.body: Trace the initial rows, one recursive round, and the stopping point. Check whether the starting employee should be included.

sections.title: Recap
sections.body: Define the starting set, the next-step rule, and a termination strategy; order the final result explicitly.
